visits.text: The Kiruna→Abisko road (95 km) runs along Lake Torneträsk, Scandinavia's largest mountain lake – 330 km² of glacial water framed by peaks. In clear weather, you'll glimpse Lapporten (Čuonjávággi in Northern Sami), the U-shaped glacial valley that's one of Lapland's symbols.

Abisko National Park, founded in 1909, covers 77 km². Start at the Naturum, the park information centre. In the afternoon, follow the Abiskojåkka canyon trail – allow an hour for the short route there and back. The river has carved a deep gorge in the rock. Climb towards the mountains from Abisko Turiststation for the most impressive viewpoints.

From Abisko Turiststation, follow the Kungsleden – the King's Trail, which crosses Swedish Lapland all the way to Hemavan. For a hike of a few hours, walk the first section through birch forest and along the Abiskojåkka, then turn back whenever you wish. Experienced hikers can continue to Lake Abiskojaure, about 14 km from Abisko: the roughly 28 km round trip then makes for a long day of hiking. Bring good footwear and equipment suitable for rapidly changing weather.

Third day in Abisko – take your time. You've driven for two weeks to get here; now it's time to catch your breath. The wooden sauna by Lake Torneträsk (book at Abisko Turiststation that morning) is one of the journey's most memorable experiences – especially if you alternate sauna sessions with a plunge into the glacial lake.

activities.text: If you're here from September to March, the Aurora Sky Station on Mount Nuolja is the place to go in the evening. Chairlift to 900 m, panoramic terrace and heated café. Abisko benefits from a microclimate called the “blue hole”: the mountains create a clear-sky zone even when it's raining in Kiruna. In summer, the same chairlift takes you up to see the midnight sun. Book ahead.

If you prefer a short and easy hike, follow the loop along the Abiskojåkka from Abisko Turiststation. Over roughly 3.5 km, the trail crosses birch forest and follows the river and its canyon, with several viewpoints over the national park landscape. Take time to observe the local birds and Arctic vegetation: it is an excellent alternative for enjoying Abisko without setting out on a long day of walking.

In summer, guided hikes to the summit of Nuolja (1,164 m) depart in the evening from the Aurora Sky Station to see the midnight sun. In winter, this is where you have the best chance of seeing the northern lights on the entire trip. Otherwise, rest, read, wander freely – Abisko is a place where doing nothing is perfectly legitimate.

visits.text: At about 9 m high and over 60 m in diameter, Anundshög is Sweden’s largest burial mound. Remains of a fire found beneath the mound date to between 210 and 540 CE, but the mound’s exact age remains disputed. Five stone ships surround it: standing stones outline the shape of a hull on the ground. The largest is over 50 m long. The site also served as a meeting place for the thing, the assembly where regional affairs were settled. In summer, guided tours are offered Monday through Friday.

“Folkvid raised all these stones for his son Heden, Anund’s brother”: this is the text on Anundshög’s large runestone. It stands in the middle of a row of 15 standing stones alongside the mound. The inscription also states that Vred carved the runes. This row appears to mark the Eriksgata, the journey each new king of Sweden made in the Middle Ages to have his election confirmed by the provincial assemblies. Walk along the row to see how the stones align.

visits.text: Åre is Sweden's main mountain resort – and one of Scandinavia's most important. In winter, it's the country's most popular alpine ski area, host of the Alpine World Ski Championships (1954, 2007, 2019). In summer, the crowds vanish and the village returns to a human scale: a few lively streets, restaurants, a central square where hikers and mountain bikers mingle.

The Kabinbanan cable car climbs in 7 minutes from the central square (421 m) to the upper station at 1274 m – 853 m elevation gain in cabins accommodating 75 people. From the station, an additional 30-minute walk leads to Åreskutan summit (1420 m) and Toppstugan – Sweden's highest café, operating since 1892, where they serve waffles without running water or electricity (everything is carried up by hand). The panorama from up there over Jämtland's ranges is the perfect endpoint for this circuit.

The village of Fröå Gruva, east of Åreskutan, marks the site of an old mine surrounded by hiking and cross-country ski trails. A little away from the main tourist routes, it's a quiet way to end the day before catching the train.

activities.text: Åre is renowned for downhill mountain biking – the lifts operate in summer to take riders uphill. Local operators offer bike hire and downhill lessons. If you're not a mountain biker, the marked hiking trails around the massif offer 5–15 km loops with beautiful views over Lake Åresjön below.

Åre is connected by train to Östersund (1 hour) and Stockholm (6 hours 30 minutes), as well as to Storlien and Norway to the west (30 minutes to the border). If you continue to Norway, the train journey through the Jämtland valley is one of the country's most beautiful – plan to sit by the window.

visits.text: At the top of Majberget, a wooded hill in Bengtsfors, Gammelgården brings together more than 20 historic houses. This open-air museum, the largest in western Sweden, features a prosperous farmer’s homestead, a miller’s house, and a soldier’s house. A house from Nössemark, built in the 1850s, was reassembled here in 1929. The grounds are freely accessible: stroll among the houses when you arrive in the evening. In summer, guided tours sometimes provide access to the interiors for 100 kronor.

days_plan.itin_title: Värmland and Dalsland in 4 Days: Canal, Aqueduct, and Forests

visits.text: The Carl Johans slussar lock staircase at Berg is probably the most famous on the Göta Canal. Seven adjoining locks raise boats 18.8 m from Lake Roxen to Berg harbor. The principle is simple. Each lock is a chamber closed off by watertight gates. The boat enters, the gate closes behind it, and water from the chamber above fills its chamber, raising it one step. Here, the upper gate of one chamber serves as the lower gate of the next. Allow 1 hour to follow a boat from bottom to top.

From the outside, Vreta klosters kyrka, the church of the former Vreta convent, looks like a village church. Yet it houses the tombs of four Swedish kings. One of them, Inge the Elder, founded the country’s first convent here with Queen Helena in the early 12th century. The convent later joined the Cistercian order, a religious order from France. Its ruins extend north of the church and are accessible at any time. It is a 300 m detour from the canal path. The church is open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on weekdays.

activities.text: Walk along the dragväg, the towpath once used to pull boats along the Göta Canal. Between Berg and Borensberg, it runs for about 20 km, with no cars. Along the way, a stone erected in 1932 honors the 58,000 soldiers who dug the canal. You will also pass Dubbelgångaren, “the Double,” a 9 m sculpture of rusted iron installed in 2006. Berg’s bascule bridge, built in 1998, offers an unobstructed view of Lake Roxen. The Kaffeteriet café rents bicycles in Berg and Borensberg.

days_plan.itin_title: Göta Canal in 3 Days: Berg Locks, Vadstena, and Omberg

visits.text: The guided tour, included in the boat ticket, is the best way to understand Birka, a Viking town on the island of Björkö. Founded around 750, Birka was a hub of Viking trade until it was abandoned around 975. Over 45 to 60 minutes, the guide leads you through a cemetery of burial mounds, graves beneath mounds of earth, up to the Borg, the former hillfort. The tour ends near the cross dedicated to Ansgar, the monk who founded Sweden’s first Christian community here in 831. The entire tour takes place outdoors: wear sturdy shoes.

In 2017, DNA analysis changed the story of Birka’s grave Bj 581. The warrior buried there with a sword, an ax, arrows, and two horses was a woman. Some researchers still debate this finding because the objects from the grave, excavated in the 1870s, had been moved. The grave lies near the guided tour route, beside the site of the former garrison: ask your guide to point it out.

The Birka Museum presents what excavations have revealed about the town. Of the more than 3,000 graves identified on the island, about a third have been excavated. At its peak, Birka had around 700 inhabitants, making it the size of a large village today. Allow 20 minutes to 1 hour for your visit, and pick up the free island map there before setting off on your own for Ansgar’s Chapel.

Goats and chickens roam among the houses in Birka’s reconstructed Viking quarter. You can also see Viking boats and an herb garden. Guides and staff wear Viking costumes. In July, the Vikingar på Birka festival (Vikings at Birka) brings the island to life for three weeks: this is the best time to visit with children.

activities.text: Walk 15 to 25 minutes to Ansgar’s Chapel, built in the 1930s and open throughout the season. It is named after the monk who came to preach Christianity in Birka around 830. The island also has a beach and rocks where you can swim: bring a swimsuit on hot days. Keep an eye on the time, as you have between 3 hours and 3 hours 30 minutes on the island before the return boat.

visits.text: Bönhamn is the High Coast’s best-loved old fishing village. Its tightly clustered boathouses surround a small, naturally sheltered harbor. Fishing was long the main source of income here. Today, this is where the boat to the island of Högbonden departs. Stroll along the docks toward the end of the day, once the day visitors have left. A harbor café also serves lunch, and there is a fee for parking in the village.

Next, stop by Bönhamn Chapel, a small fishermen’s chapel. It was not built here. In the 16th century, fishermen from Gävle, a coastal town farther south, leased these fishing waters. They built the chapel on the islet of Höglosmen, north of Högbonden. In the early 19th century, it was dismantled and reassembled in Bönhamn, on the mainland. In winter, it was also used to store fishing equipment. Admission is free, and concerts are held here in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: High Coast in 3 Days: Skuleberget, Ulvön, and Högbonden

visits.text: Borgholm Castle is an imposing ruin atop a rocky plateau overlooking the sea. Begun in the 16th century and expanded until the 18th, it burned in 1806 and was never rebuilt. Its ochre sandstone walls and gutted towers have a romantic allure. The interior is open to visitors, and summer concerts are held here.

Solliden Royal Palace, the Swedish royal family's summer residence since 1906, has gardens that are partly open to visitors. The private apartments remain closed, but the French-style parterres and flower-filled terraces are worth visiting.

Stora Alvaret is a limestone steppe extending over 260 km² in the centre and south of the island. This almost lunar landscape - short grass, exposed rocks, wild orchids in spring - is one of the rare examples of this ecosystem in Europe. It earned Öland its UNESCO World Heritage listing in 2000. From Borgholm, allow for a day trip to explore the plateau and return.

The Ottenby bird reserve, at the southern tip of the island, is one of Scandinavia's most important migration sites. More than 300 species have been recorded here. At the end of the headland, Långe Jan - “Long John” - is Sweden's tallest lighthouse at 41 metres. From Borgholm, allow for a day trip to visit the reserve and lighthouse and return.

Öland has several hundred windmills, including around forty still standing along the east coast. The most accessible are around Lerkaka, where five windmills stand side by side in a meadow. From Borgholm, allow for a round trip by road to Lerkaka.

activities.text: Öland is completely flat - it is the ideal island for cycling. Rental shops in Borgholm offer bicycles for exploring southwards. The cycle path follows the east coast for several dozen kilometres.
Birdwatching at dawn at Ottenby: in spring and autumn, the migrations of cranes, geese and birds of prey are spectacular from sunrise. From Borgholm, allow for the round trip by road for this outing.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand South: From Malmö to Stockholm via the Islands

visits.text: The king and queen of Sweden still live at Drottningholm Palace: they have occupied the south wing since 1981. The rest of the palace is open to visitors. After the old castle burned down, Queen Hedvig Eleonora commissioned architect Nicodemus Tessin the Elder to rebuild it, beginning in 1662. UNESCO, which inscribed it on the World Heritage List in 1991, describes it as inspired by Versailles. From June through August, a 45-minute guided tour in English starts daily at 11:30 a.m. and 2:30 p.m.

The Swedes call it Kina slott, the “Chinese Castle”: it is the Chinese Pavilion tucked away at the far end of Drottningholm’s park. One evening in July 1753, King Adolf Fredrik surprised Queen Lovisa Ulrika with it as a birthday gift. He had it built in secret. Several rooms retain their original silk and Chinese paper wall coverings, alongside Swedish furniture imitating the Chinese style. The pavilion opens only in summer: save it for the end of your walk through the park.

Thunder still rumbles at the Slottsteater, the Drottningholm Palace Theater, but it comes from a wooden machine. The theater, which opened in 1766, has retained its original stage machinery, still operated by hand: a wave machine, a thunder machine, and a flying chair that lifts actors into the air. This system allows rapid scenery changes with the curtain raised, in full view of the audience. After King Gustav III’s assassination in 1792, the theater was used for furniture storage before being rediscovered in 1921. The guided tour in English lasts about 1 hour and runs from May through early October (150 SEK).

activities.text: The grounds of Drottningholm Palace deserve as much time as its state rooms. In front of the facade, the Baroque garden created by the two Tessin architects, father and son, features geometric flower beds. Farther north, Gustav III began an English landscape garden, a landscaped park that imitates nature instead of trimming it into straight lines. The park is open year-round, day and night, and admission is free: enjoy it while waiting for your guided tour.

visits.text: In 1856, a fire destroyed half of Eksjö but spared the northern part of its wooden old town. This district, Gamla stan, is lined with wooden houses from the 17th and 18th centuries and has numerous courtyards. Almost the entire old town has protected heritage status. Eksjö has also received the Europa Nostra Award, a European distinction for heritage conservation. In summer, the town museum organizes guided walks.

Eksjö museum tells the story of the town’s 600-year history in the heart of the old town. The top floor is devoted to Albert Engström (1869–1940), an illustrator known for caricatures that mocked the failings of his time. Another room traces Eksjö’s military past. The town was long nicknamed the “town of hussars,” after these army cavalrymen. Then take a break in the courtyard, where an herb garden runs alongside the river.

To see how the upper classes lived in a small Swedish town in the 19th century, step inside Aschanska gården. The Aschan family, whose members included manufacturers and judges, lived here for three generations, from the 1830s until 1984. The entire interior of this upper-middle-class home has been preserved. Guided tours run daily in summer: book through Eksjö museum, which organizes them.

activities.text: Even in midsummer, the air turns cool at the bottom of Skurugata, a rocky gorge 800 m long and 7 m wide in places, 10 km northeast of Eksjö. In some years, snow and ice have lingered here into summer. Its origins are still debated: the most common explanation points to two parallel fractures in the rock. A 2 km loop starts at the parking lot, passes the Skuruhatt viewpoint, then descends into the gorge.

visits.text: Gothenburg locals call it Feskekôrka, “the fish church” in the local dialect. The nickname comes from the shape of the building, which opened in 1874: with its tall, pointed windows, it looks like a church. It is, however, Gothenburg’s fish market. After four years of restoration, it reopened in May 2024 with fishmongers’ counters, lunch deals, and two restaurants upstairs. Come at noon and eat overlooking the canal on one of the city’s largest terraces.

visits.text: Huge boulders wedged above your head form a stone roof: Kungsklyftan is a roughly 200-meter-long cleft that splits Vetteberget hill in Fjällbacka in two. Its name means “the king’s cleft.” It commemorates King Oscar II’s visit in 1887, when he left his signature on the rock face at the northern entrance. Scenes from the film adaptation of Astrid Lindgren’s novel Ronia, the Robber’s Daughter were filmed here. The passage is steep, so wear closed-toe shoes.

Despite its small size, the fishing village of Fjällbacka attracted a Hollywood star. Starting in 1958, actress Ingrid Bergman spent every summer on Dannholmen, a nearby islet. After her death in 1982, her ashes were scattered around the island, and a bust of her was later unveiled in the village. The central square, Ingrid Bergmans torg, bears her name. Novelist Camilla Läckberg, who was born in Fjällbacka, sets several of her crime novels here: start at the square to recognize their settings.

In the mid-18th century, herring brought prosperity to Fjällbacka. Around 1850, the village was the busiest fishing port in its region. According to the tourist office, Swedish ansjovis originated at a cannery in Fjällbacka. Despite its name, it is made with sprats, small relatives of herring, rather than anchovies, and cured in brine for several months. Walk along the quay: you can explore the old village, squeezed between the hill and the sea, in 30 minutes.

activities.text: Climb the Vetteberget stairs from Ingrid Bergmans torg: at 74 meters, the hill towers over Fjällbacka. From the summit, views stretch across the harbor, the archipelago’s islands, and the inland countryside. The Vettebergsleden loop trail, marked in blue, is 4 km long and also passes through Kungsklyftan. It is steep in places, but numerous steps make the climb easier. At the trailhead, a QR code provides access to an audio guide to the trail.

days_plan.itin_title: Bohuslän in 4 Days: Marstrand, Smögen, Tanum, and Koster

visits.text: The building is old; the images are new. Fotografiska, a photography museum that opened in 2010, occupies a former brick customs house built in 1906 in the Art Nouveau style. Its temporary exhibitions change throughout the year. Then head to the top floor: according to the tourist office, its café offers one of Stockholm’s finest panoramic views. The museum is open every day until 11 p.m., so save it for the evening.

days_plan.itin_title: Stockholm in 2 Days: Gamla Stan, the Vasa Museum, and Skansen

visits.text: Funäsdalen is the hub of life in mountainous Härjedalen: a mountain village at the foot of Funäsdalsberget, surrounded by over 30 peaks exceeding 1000 m in the area. The Härjedalens Fjällmuseum, inaugurated in 1999, is one of Sweden's most modern museums. Its beautiful exhibitions present the region's history through mountain farmers, Sami people and craftspeople – its collections are among the country's oldest. It received a special mention at the 2001 European Museum of the Year Awards.

Push on to Tännäs, about twenty kilometres east, to see the musk oxen at Myskoxcentrum. In 1971, five musk oxen spontaneously crossed the Norwegian border and settled in the mountains west of Tännäs – forming the basis of the current herd. The centre, created in 2010, offers guided visits at a respectful distance. These animals, covered in their thick woolly coats, look like something out of prehistory – because that's exactly what they are. Book ahead.

activities.text: Funäsdalsberget (the mountain just above the village) offers a half-day hike accessible to all. From the summit, the view extends as far as Sylarna in the north and Sonfjället in the south – a panorama taking in 30 peaks. In summer, the ski runs transform into marked trails.

Nordic Ski Center (NSC) at Funäsfjällen claims one of the world's longest groomed cross-country ski networks, with 300 km of trails. In summer, these same trails become mountain bike and hiking paths. Outfitters offer mountain bike rentals on-site.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: Gällivare is a mining town of 10,000 inhabitants set in the tundra. The Aitik copper mine, 15 km to the south, forms a crater 3 km long and 450 m deep. Guided tours are available in summer. In Malmberget, the neighbouring mining village, the same phenomenon as in Kiruna is occurring: the ground is subsiding and part of the village is being relocated.

Dundret (820 m), the mountain overlooking Gällivare, offers a 360° panorama over forests, lakes and tundra. It's one of Lapland's best places to observe the midnight sun (late May to mid-July): a paved road climbs almost to the summit. In winter, Dundret is also an aurora viewing spot.

activities.text: Muddus National Park is one of Europe's last remaining primeval forests - 700-year-old pines, peat bogs and the Muddusfallet waterfall (a 42 m drop). Plan a return trip during the day from Gällivare to the car park. The walk to the waterfall (7 km one way) is worth the effort.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

activities.text: Take time to get lost in Gamla Stan, the old town founded in the 13th century on the island of Stadsholmen. At its center, Stortorget square was the site of the “Stockholm Bloodbath.” In November 1520, King Christian II of Denmark had 90 people executed there over three days, mostly Swedish nobles. On the square, the former Stock Exchange houses the Nobel Prize Museum. Then walk down the 36 steps of Mårten Trotzigs gränd, Stockholm’s narrowest alley: just 90 cm at its narrowest point. It starts on Prästgatan.

days_plan.itin_title: Stockholm in 2 Days: Gamla Stan, the Vasa Museum, and Skansen

visits.text: Gävle is the home of the Gävlebocken, the world's most famous straw Christmas goat. Every first Sunday of Advent since 1966, a giant goat standing 13 metres tall and made of 3.6 tonnes of straw has been erected. The problem: vandals regularly set it on fire before Christmas. In 2001, an American tourist burned it down, believing this was a legal tradition - he spent 18 days in prison. The goat even has its own Twitter account. If you visit in December, you will see it (perhaps).

Gamla Gefle is the old fishing quarter - colourful wooden houses from the 18th century, narrow lanes and a village atmosphere in the middle of the city. It survived the fire of 1869, which destroyed much of Gävle.

The Swedish Railway Museum (Sveriges Järnvägsmuseum) is the country's largest railway museum – 19th-century steam locomotives, royal carriages, and a reconstructed station from 1900. Even if you're not a train enthusiast, the exhibition design is worth the visit. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

activities.text: Boulognerskogen park, in the city centre, is one of northern Sweden's finest urban parks – tall trees, a river, and open-air concerts in summer. If you have the campervan, several parking areas are accessible on the city outskirts.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

activities.text: A canoe offers the best view of Glaskogen. Established in 1970, this nature reserve covers nearly 29,000 ha of forests and lakes between Arvika and Årjäng. Its name means “Gla Forest.” Its two largest lakes are Stora Gla and Övre Gla. At Lenungshammar, in the heart of the reserve, the rental center provides canoes, paddles, and life jackets. To get started, choose the easy Buvatten route, which takes 2 to 3 hours. Avoid Övre Gla in windy weather: this large lake can turn choppy in minutes.

Next, follow the 5 km loop trail that starts at the Lenungshammar reception center. Its first section is suitable for strollers and wheelchairs. Glaskogen has around 300 km of trails marked in orange, with wooden shelters and cabins for overnight stays. Loons, large waterbirds that dive for fish, nest near several lakes. In summer, Café Carl, right by the reception center, is a good place for a break before hitting the road.

days_plan.itin_title: Värmland and Dalsland in 4 Days: Canal, Aqueduct, and Forests

visits.text: A water-filled moat, a drawbridge, and bare stone walls: Glimmingehus looks like a storybook fortress set amid the fields. The Danish knight Jens Holgersen Ulfstand had it built between 1499 and 1506. Its architect, the German stonemason Adam van Düren, had also worked on Lund Cathedral. The Swedish National Heritage Board describes it as the best-preserved medieval castle in the Nordic countries. Admission costs 100 kronor and is free for visitors ages 18 and under.

activities.text: Take the guided tour of Glimmingehus, included in your ticket, to spot the castle’s traps. False doors and dead-end corridors awaited attackers. Through holes above the passageways, defenders poured boiling pitch, a heated resin, onto anyone forcing their way in. The walls are 2.4 m thick at the base. From July 1 to August 9, an English-language tour departs daily at 12:30 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Skåne in 4 Days: Lund, Helsingborg, Kullaberg, and Österlen

visits.text: In 1923, Gothenburg celebrated its 300th anniversary, and Göteborgs konstmuseum, the city's art museum, was completed for the occasion. It stands at the top of the main avenue, with a facade of yellow brick known as “Gothenburg brick.” Inside, the Fürstenberg Gallery, named after a couple who donated to the museum, brings together Nordic painters from the late 19th century, from Carl Larsson to Edvard Munch. The collection also ranges from Rembrandt to Picasso, including Van Gogh and Monet. On weekends, it is open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; admission is 75 SEK, free for visitors under 20.

If you take just one photo at Götaplatsen, make it Poseidon, Carl Milles's fountain statue in the center of the square. Unveiled in 1931, it has become one of Gothenburg's symbols. Around it stand the art museum, the city theater, and the concert hall, where the Gothenburg Symphony Orchestra performs. The best vantage point is at the top of the museum steps, with Kungsportsavenyen in the background.

days_plan.itin_title: Gothenburg in 2 Days: Haga, Canals, Liseberg, and Styrsö

visits.text: Göteborgs naturhistoriska museum, the city's natural history museum, stands on a hill in Slottsskogen. Its star attraction is a young blue whale nearly 16 meters long that washed ashore near Gothenburg in 1865. Its skin was stretched over a wooden frame. The West Sweden tourist board describes it as the world's only taxidermied blue whale on display. Visitors once entered its belly, which was fitted with benches. Today, its jaw opens only on special occasions, such as election days. Admission is 70 SEK, free for visitors under 20; closed Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Gothenburg in 2 Days: Haga, Canals, Liseberg, and Styrsö

visits.text: On July 11, 1897, explorer Salomon August Andrée, born in Gränna, took off from Svalbard with two companions in a hydrogen balloon, intending to fly over the North Pole. The balloon landed on the sea ice just over two days later, and the three men never returned. Their remains were found in 1930 on White Island (Kvitøya). Grenna Museum displays their belongings, photographs, and a replica of their ice shelter. In summer, it is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., with admission costing 80 kronor per adult.

The layout of Brahegatan, Gränna’s main street, was no accident. Count Per Brahe the Younger founded the town in 1652 and aligned its streets toward his Brahehus Castle on the hill. Amalia Eriksson, who invented the local candy sticks, lived at number 2. Andrée’s birthplace is at number 37. Then climb Grännaberget, the hill above town: its open-air museum, dating from 1912, brings together historic buildings and offers free admission.

On a clear day, head up to Brahehus to see Lake Vättern and the island of Visingsö at your feet, 180 m below. Count Per Brahe the Younger had this castle built in the 17th century. A fire that spread from the neighboring village of Uppgränna destroyed it in 1708. The ruins, 3 km from Gränna, are accessible free of charge day and night, right beside a service area on the E4 highway.

activities.text: Swedes call it “polkagris,” literally “polka pig”: at the time, “gris” was a colloquial word for candy, and the polka was the fashionable dance. This red-and-white candy stick was invented in Gränna in 1859 by Amalia Eriksson. About a dozen candy shops in town make it before your eyes. The sugar is cooked to around 150 °C, then pulled: the air worked into it turns it white, and it is twisted by hand.

days_plan.itin_title: Småland in 4 Days: Crystal, Astrid Lindgren, and Lake Vättern

visits.text: The STF Grövelsjön Fjällstation stands at an altitude of 816 m on the slopes of Långfjället, at the northern tip of Dalarna, right beside the Norwegian border. It's one of the STF (Swedish Tourist Association) mountain stations – with accommodation, a restaurant and a shop. Settle in: you're at the gateway to an exceptional hiking area with few visitors.

Lake Grövelsjön itself stretches like a banana for 15 km, straddling the Swedish-Norwegian border – its northern end lies in Norway. From Sjöstugan, 1.5 km from the mountain station, a boat crosses to Sylen on the Norwegian shore (a crossing of about 40 minutes). You'll pass into Norway without noticing – the border runs right through the middle of the lake.

The Linnaeus Trail (Linnéstigen) starts from Sjöstugan and climbs towards Norway following the exact route taken by botanist Carl Linnaeus in 1734 during his journey through Dalarna. On Långfjället, a sign marks the spot where Linnaeus observed falconers capturing wild falcons to train them for hunting – a remnant of a falconers' camp whose ruins still survive.

activities.text: The hike to the summit of Storvätteshågna (1204 m) is the day's major excursion – the highest point in Svealand, with a dizzying panorama over Norwegian fells, Töfsingdalen and the Helags massif to the north. Expect a 24 km round trip from the mountain station, taking roughly 7–8 hours. If you leave at 8am, you have plenty of time. The final ascent from Fosksjöarna is the steepest section.

For a more relaxed day, take the morning boat from Sjöstugan to Sylen (Norway), then walk back via the Linnaeus Trail (9 km back along the lake, easy terrain). You “enter” Norway without a passport, without customs, without anything – just a name change on the map. Silverfallet, a pretty waterfall 7 km from the mountain station, is an even shorter alternative.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: Haga is a neighborhood that makes you want to slow down, with its small shops, antique dealers, and cafés. Queen Christina had it laid out in the mid-17th century as Gothenburg’s first suburb, home to sailors and dockworkers. On Haga Nygata, the main pedestrian street, the buildings have a stone ground floor and two wooden stories above. These workers’ apartment buildings, known as landshövdingehus, complied with fire regulations that prohibited more than two wooden stories. During Advent, the four weeks before Christmas, the street becomes a Christmas market on weekends.

activities.text: If you try just one thing in Haga, order a hagabulle at Café Husaren, at 28 Haga Nygata. It’s a giant cinnamon bun that Gothenburg’s tourist office describes as probably the largest in the world. In Sweden, this coffee break with a pastry is called fika. One bun is easily enough for two to share: ask for two cups.

days_plan.itin_title: Gothenburg in 2 Days: Haga, Canals, Liseberg, and Styrsö

visits.text: At Håverud, the Dalsland Canal had to cross a river with powerful rapids between very steep rock faces. Building conventional locks here was impossible. Engineer Nils Ericson therefore carried the canal over the river in an aqueduct: a steel-plate trough about 33 m long that spans the rapids. Boats float in this trough while the river flows beneath it. Higher still, a railroad bridge and a road bridge cross overhead. Arrive around 10 a.m. to see it before boarding the boat.

Small museum, big story: Kanalmuseet, the canal museum, has occupied the former Håverud factory office since 1971. It shows life along the Upperud River before and after the canal. Built from 1864 to 1868, the Dalsland Canal connects lakes over around 250 km. Only about 10 km had to be excavated. Its 31 locks raise boats a total of 66 m. The museum is open daily from June through August; adult admission costs 50 kronor.

Upperud Lock, close to Håverud, deserves a visit: the tourist office ranks it among the most beautiful on the canal. Its two chambers raise or lower boats by 5 m. The canal company, Dalslands Kanal AB, has its headquarters here. In summer, a former lakeside warehouse houses a small museum and a café. A ten-minute walk away, Dalslands konstmuseum, the Dalsland art museum, displays works related to nature; check its hours before visiting.

activities.text: Board at Håverud at 10:50 a.m. for the Halva Kanalrundan, the “half-canal cruise,” to Långbron. The boat passes through 10 locks, including the four consecutive locks at Håverud, which overcome an elevation difference of 9.9 m. It also crosses the aqueduct. Built in 1868, this aqueduct is held together by 33,000 rivets, none of which have needed replacing. The company operates two boats: M/S Storholmen, built in 1896, and M/S Dalslandia, which arrived on the canal in 1973. Around 2 p.m., a railcar—a small motorized train—takes you from Långbron back to Håverud.

days_plan.itin_title: Värmland and Dalsland in 4 Days: Canal, Aqueduct, and Forests

visits.text: Helsingborg’s best viewpoint is 35 m up, at the top of Kärnan, the brick keep overlooking the city. It was built in the 1310s for the king of Denmark. It is the only surviving part of a large Danish fortress, demolished on the orders of the king of Sweden starting in the 1680s. Its walls are 4.5 m thick at the base. From the top, you can see Helsingør, Denmark, 4 km away across the Øresund.

Rådhuset, Helsingborg’s city hall, is recognizable by its tall clock tower and richly decorated red brick facades. Inaugurated in 1897, it was designed by Alfred Hellerström, who combined Italian, Dutch, and German influences. The same architect had restored Kärnan a few years earlier. Inside, ten stained-glass windows based on designs by painter Gustaf Cederström tell the city’s history. Allow twenty minutes to walk around the building and view its facades.

A great astronomer left his mark on Sankta Maria kyrka, St. Mary’s Church in Helsingborg. Tycho Brahe, the 16th-century Danish scholar, had an epitaph, or funerary plaque, installed here for his daughter Kristina, who died of the plague in 1576. This red brick Gothic church was completed around 1450. Its altarpiece, a large carved panel behind the altar, comes from Germany. Its pulpit, the raised platform from which sermons are delivered, was carved in 1615. For a guided tour, contact the parish in advance.

If it rains, take shelter at Dunkers kulturhus, Helsingborg’s cultural center, which opened in 2002. Designed by Danish architect Kim Utzon, it houses the city museum, which traces Helsingborg’s history from the Ice Age to the present day. The building also hosts art exhibitions. It is named after industrialist Henry Dunker (1870–1962), whose foundation funded it. Check the program online: temporary exhibitions change regularly.

Helsingborg’s most enjoyable museum may well be outdoors: Fredriksdal, which opened in 1923 around an 18th-century manor house. In the 1960s, houses and shops from the city center were dismantled and rebuilt here, brick by brick. Herb, rose, and wildflower gardens surround the buildings, as does an open-air theater in the French Baroque style. The park remains accessible year-round, while opening seasons vary for the buildings. Tickets start at 120 kronor.

activities.text: You’ll return the car in Helsingborg before heading to Knutpunkten, “the crossroads,” the city’s main station, which brings together trains, buses, and ferries. Ferries to Helsingør, Denmark, cross the Øresund in about 20 minutes, with more than 70 departures a day. Regional Øresundståg trains also connect Helsingborg with Copenhagen. Around 50,000 travelers pass through Knutpunkten each day: arrive early during rush hour.

visits.text: There is no better gateway to the High Coast than Högakustenbron, the High Coast Bridge. Opened in 1997, it spans the mouth of the Ångermanälven River for 1,867 m. Its two towers rise about 180 m above the water. Between them, the roadway stretches 1,210 m without any supports beneath it, suspended from large cables. Stop at the Hornöberget rest area at the north end of the bridge for a view taking in both the bridge and the river. If traveling by train, get off at Härnösand station, about 25 km to the south.

days_plan.itin_title: High Coast in 3 Days: Skuleberget, Ulvön, and Högbonden

visits.text: If the sea is calm, the M/S Ronja boat takes you to Högbonden, a steep island off Bönhamn, in 15 minutes. Its lighthouse, first lit in 1909, is the second-highest in Sweden by elevation: its light shines 75 m above the sea. Three keepers worked here when it opened. At its peak, 21 people lived on the island, and a classroom occupied the attic. The keepers’ houses now accommodate a hostel. In 2026, it was open on weekends from May 29 to June 21, daily from June 22 to August 16, and then on weekends again from August 17 to September 27. The café was open daily from June 22 to August 16.

activities.text: Walk around Högbonden along the nature reserve’s trails. The terrain is hilly and covered with stones. The island’s rock splits easily, and the sea has carved caves into it. The largest, Bondstugan, opens onto the shore just south of the lighthouse. The soil is thin everywhere: the island has been gradually rising out of the sea since the end of the Ice Age, and waves have washed away the soil as it emerged. Wear sturdy shoes and allow plenty of time before the last boat.

days_plan.itin_title: High Coast in 3 Days: Skuleberget, Ulvön, and Högbonden

visits.text: Three large grass-covered mounds stand in a row north of Adelsö Church: these are the Kungshögar, the “Kings’ Mounds” of Hovgården. They are part of a group of five large burial mounds, graves covered by a mound of earth. Hovgården was already a royal estate during the Viking Age, which lasted from about 800 to 1050. Together with Birka, on the neighboring island, the site has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1993. Visit it before boarding the boat, as the drive to Mariefred awaits when you return.

Only ruins remain of Alsnö hus, the brick palace that King Magnus Ladulås had built at Hovgården in the 1270s. Yet it was here that he issued the Ordinance of Alsnö in 1279. This decree exempted anyone who supplied the king with a heavily armed horseman from land tax. These exempt families formed the Swedish nobility. Nearby stands runestone U 11, carved in the 11th century with runes, the Viking alphabet. Its inscription says that a steward named Tolir had it carved for the king.

activities.text: To reach Hovgården, take the free Adelsöleden ferry, which connects the islands of Munsö and Adelsö in 6 minutes. Allow about another 10 minutes to drive to the parking lot at the hembygdsgård, the local heritage center. The dock for the boat to Birka is at least a 15-minute walk away along a gravel path through a cow pasture. This path is not recommended for people with limited mobility.

The boat from Birka takes you back to the Hovgården dock on the island of Adelsö. Walk back up to the parking lot, at least 15 minutes away, then take the Adelsöleden ferry back toward Munsö. The drive to Mariefred takes you through Ekerö again: allow nearly two hours, including the ferry crossing.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake Mälaren in 3 Days: Drottningholm, Birka, and Gripsholm
Lake Mälaren in 3 Days: Drottningholm, Birka, and Gripsholm

visits.text: Idre is a small village set close to the Norwegian border in northwestern Dalarna. The surrounding region is fjäll country – those bare high plateaus above the treeline characteristic of Scandinavia. Take time to drive slowly as you arrive: the landscape shifts gradually from dense forest to bare, windswept ridges.

Städjan-Nipfjället Nature Reserve is worth a detour. Nipfjället reaches 1,192 m, and the 16 km² reserve was created in 1974 (expanded in 2010) to protect unique Arctic flora and fauna: reindeer, foxes and many species of mountain birds of prey. The distinctive, volcano-shaped silhouette of nearby Städjan (1,131 m) can be seen from afar.

activities.text: The circular hike up Städjan (6 km, ~380 m elevation gain) from the Nipstugan car park is the region's flagship excursion. The 360° panorama from the summit takes in Norwegian fells to the west and Dalarna's forests to the east. Allow 2.5–3 hours. The trail is well marked but the terrain is rocky on the upper section – good walking shoes are essential.

Shorter alternative: the ascent to Lillnipen (1100 m), starting from the upper Nipfjället car park, 1.5 km round trip. Very easy, perfect if you just want to feel the fjäll wind without exertion. The view over the Härjedalen fells to the east and Fulufjället to the west is well worth the minimal effort.

Idre Fjäll, the ski resort a few kilometres north of the village, offers 25 marked mountain bike trails in summer including the famous Städjan DH (rated black). Outfitters rent equipment on-site. It's one of Sweden's best-known MTB parks.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: Just before Jokkmokk, you cross the Arctic Circle on the E45 – a signposted roadside marker where you can take photos. North of this line, the sun doesn't rise in winter and doesn't set in summer.

Ájtte Museum is Sweden's national museum of Sami culture. Its name means “storehouse” in Lule Sami. You'll see exhibitions on Sami nomadic life, reindeer herding, joik (Sami singing), ceremonial drums and costumes. It's Sweden's most comprehensive Sami museum. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes.

Jokkmokk's winter market has been held from the first Thursday to the following Saturday in February since 1605 - more than 400 years without interruption. King Karl IX decreed the creation of markets in Lapland to collect taxes and spread Christianity. Today, 30,000 to 40,000 visitors descend on this town of 3,000 inhabitants for three days of Sami crafts and reindeer races on the frozen lake. If you are not here in February, the small red Sami church with its separate bell tower recalls this history.

activities.text: Jokkmokk is the gateway to Laponia, a 9,400 km² UNESCO site comprising Muddus, Padjelanta, Sarek and Stora Sjöfallet national parks. Local operators offer guided outings in the boreal forest around the village.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

activities.text: End the trip in Jönköping, 31 minutes from Gränna via the E4 highway. The station’s transportation hub, the resecentrum, brings together trains and intercity buses. Regional trains run to Nässjö, Växjö, and Gothenburg via Falköping. SJ trains also depart for Stockholm. Jönköping Airport has had no scheduled flights since 2020: to fly home, travel through another city.

days_plan.itin_title: Småland in 4 Days: Crystal, Astrid Lindgren, and Lake Vättern

visits.text: Kalmar Castle is one of Sweden's best-preserved Renaissance castles. Here in 1397 the Kalmar Union was signed, a treaty uniting Sweden, Denmark, and Norway under a single crown—a union that lasted until 1523. The castle was remodeled in the 16th century by the Vasa kings, and its restored interior halls are among Scandinavia's most lavish.

Kalmar's baroque cathedral dates from the 17th century—built to plans by Nicodemus Tessin the Elder, the Swedish royal court architect. Its yellow facade and dome are recognizable from throughout the lower town.

Old Kalmar, rebuilt after a 17th-century fire, follows a regular grid plan with low wooden houses painted red, ochre, and yellow. Walk the Kalmarsund waterfront to see traditional boats moored facing Öland island.

activities.text: In the afternoon, cross the Öland Bridge—6 km of concrete over the sea, toll-free, opened in 1972 and still Sweden's longest bridge. The drive across with views of the Kalmarsund in good weather is an experience in its own right. You can stop on Öland for an initial look around before returning to spend the night in Kalmar.
The fishing establishments at Kalmar's harbor still serve fresh Baltic fish—perch, pike, and smoked eel are the local must-tries.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand South: From Malmö to Stockholm via the Islands

visits.text: Karlskrona was founded in 1680 by King Charles XI as the main naval base for Sweden's Baltic fleet—the entire city was planned around its shipyards. It's the world's only still-operational baroque naval base, earning UNESCO World Heritage status in 1998. Start at the grand Stortorget, one of Sweden's largest baroque squares, flanked by two twin circular churches.

The Marinmuseum (Naval Museum) traces 350 years of Swedish naval history with models, cannons, uniforms, and a section on Baltic battles. Outside, you can board the submarine HMS Neptun, a real Cold War submarine open for tours—the passageways are narrow, the atmosphere claustrophobic, and it's fascinating.

The Admiralty Church (Amiralitetskyrkan), built in 1685, is the largest surviving wooden church in Sweden. Before its entrance stands a wooden statue of an old lighthouse keeper who has been begging since the 18th century—tradition calls for dropping a coin in his bowl.
Karlskrona's archipelago extends across dozens of islands and islets around the city. Local ferries reach the main inhabited islands from the central harbor—some shelter 18th-century fortifications.

activities.text: Rent a kayak from the harbor to paddle along the fortifications—the view of the city and bastions from sea level is very different from the view from the quays.
Karlskrona's covered market (Saluhallen) offers smoked Baltic fish, Swedish cheeses, and Scanian gingerbread—a good option for a quick lunch.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand South: From Malmö to Stockholm via the Islands

visits.text: Ugly, perhaps, but with a fine story to tell: the woman with the broken sword on Stora torget, Karlstad’s main square, was voted “Sweden’s ugliest statue” by a television show. Fredsmonumentet, the Peace Monument, was unveiled in 1955. It commemorates the peaceful separation of Sweden and Norway in 1905. That agreement was negotiated and signed in Karlstad. Northwest of the square, also look for the statue of Sola, an 18th-century waitress nicknamed “the sun” for her cheerful disposition.

On July 2, 1865, a fire destroyed almost all of Karlstad. Only the cathedral and a few houses remained standing. Even so, Domkyrkan, the cathedral, lost its bell tower and roof that day. It had been completed in 1730 by Christian Haller, a builder from Saxony. The tower you see today was rebuilt after the fire. Then look at the layout of the surrounding streets: after the fire, the city was rebuilt on a grid, with wide, tree-lined streets.

For us, Karlstad’s most beautiful walk crosses Östra bron, the old stone bridge. At 168 m long, with twelve arches, it is Sweden’s longest stone arch bridge. Construction took fifty years, from 1761 to 1811. Legend has it that its master builder, Anders Jacobsson, took his own life for fear the bridge would collapse. That is untrue: he died at home in 1804. The bridge is about 600 m northeast of Stora torget, over the eastern branch of the Klarälven River.

If you visit just one museum in Karlstad, choose Värmlands museum, the museum of the Värmland region. It tells the region’s story from the Ice Age onward. Since 1998, a passageway has connected the oldest building, dating from 1929, to a modern wing. The museum occupies the tip of Sandgrundsudden, beside the Klarälven River. Admission costs 120 kronor and is free for visitors age 20 and under. It opens daily, staying open until 8 p.m. on Wednesdays and Fridays.

Right next to the museum, the former Sandgrund dance hall, a restaurant where people used to come to dance, now houses the Sandgrund Lars Lerin gallery. It displays watercolors by Lars Lerin, born in Munkfors in 1954. The tourist office describes him as one of the Nordic countries’ leading watercolor artists. The paintings on display change about once a year. The gallery opens Tuesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., with admission costing 120 kronor. In summer, its terrace overlooks the river.

activities.text: At Inre hamn, the inner harbor, board a båtbuss, a water bus on the regional transit network. Karlstad is built on the delta where the Klarälven River flows into Lake Vänern. This is the largest lake in Sweden and the European Union: 5,650 km² dotted with about 22,000 islands and rocks. Route 93 takes you to the islands of Jäverön or Västra Långholmen, depending on the day. In 2026, water buses ran from June 8 to August 30, and a one-way trip cost 33 kronor.

days_plan.itin_title: Värmland and Dalsland in 4 Days: Canal, Aqueduct, and Forests

visits.text: Kiruna's LKAB mine is the world's largest underground iron ore mine. Opened in 1899, it extracts ore at a depth of over 1,365 metres along a 4 km seam. Guided tours descend by bus to level 540 – 400 km of tunnels in total. Sweden is the European Union's top iron producer thanks to this deposit. Book ahead: places sell out quickly in high season.

Kiruna's wooden church (Kiruna Kyrka), built between 1909 and 1912 by Gustaf Wickman, draws inspiration from Sami tents and Norwegian stave churches. Weighing 672 tonnes, it was voted Sweden's most beautiful building constructed before 1950. In 2025, it was moved 5 km to escape the mining subsidence zone – the entire town is being relocated eastward.

Free day in Kiruna. The town's relocation is a spectacle in itself: 'new Kiruna', 3 km east, is growing around a new central square while the old centre gradually empties. Some historic buildings are moved on trailers – others demolished. You can observe the process from signposted viewpoints in town.

Jukkasjärvi, in addition to the Icehotel, is a historic Sami village with a 17th-century wooden church whose altarpiece is the work of Bror Hjorth. Operators offer Sami cultural visits with local reindeer herders.
Return Abisko→Kiruna (95 km). Last visits or shopping in Kiruna. If you haven't yet, climb to the LKAB mine viewpoint – the crater is visible from the road.

If you still have time before your flight, enjoy one last walk along the shore of Lake Luossajärvi near Kiruna. The open views across the water, surrounding hills and distant mining facilities capture the contrast that defines the town between Arctic nature and industrial activity. It is an easy stop to adapt to your departure time.

activities.text: The Icehotel in Jukkasjärvi (17 km east), rebuilt each winter since 1989 from Torne river ice, is the world's first ice hotel. The permanent section stays open year-round through refrigeration. An hour's visit suffices to appreciate the sculptures and ephemeral architecture.

For those feeling energetic, climb Luossavaara (775 m), the mountain north of Kiruna – a former iron mine converted to a ski resort. In summer, the view from the summit takes in the town, Lake Luossajärvi and Lapland's mountains.

Last evening in Lapland. If you are travelling by campervan, choose an authorised place for your final night, ideally beside a lake or in a natural setting around Kiruna. Allemansrätten gives considerable freedom to people travelling on foot or camping in a tent, but it does not give motor vehicles the right to drive or park anywhere in nature. Follow road signs and any local restrictions.
Departure from Kiruna airport (flights to Stockholm, approximately 1 hour 30 minutes). Return the campervan or car in Kiruna. The airport is 8 km from the city centre.
