visits.text: In 1748, two farmers quarrying stone near Kivik stumbled upon a stone cist made of engraved slabs. They had just discovered Kiviksgraven, also called Kungagraven, “the king’s tomb.” This Bronze Age cairn, an enormous mound of stones raised over a tomb around 1400 BCE, measures 75 m in diameter. Inside, eight original slabs depict ships, a chariot drawn by two horses, and musicians playing the lur, a long bronze horn. The burial chamber is open to visitors only during the warmer months: check opening hours at bredaror.se.

Apple orchards line the roads: you are in the heartland of Kiviks Musteri, Kivik’s juice and cider company. Its information center, Äpplets hus (the house of the apple), opened in 1996 and tells the story of fruit growing in the village since 1888. Around 70 apple varieties grow in the orchards around Kivik. Admission is free. At the shop, sample the juices and ciders before buying.

activities.text: You will spend the evening at Kivik’s harbor, a small fishing port facing Hanö Bay. The village, with fewer than a thousand residents, is known for its apples but also for its herring. Look for it on the menus of the harbor restaurants. Every July, Kiviks marknad, a large three-day fair, takes over the streets. If your trip falls during the fair, book your overnight stay well in advance.

days_plan.itin_title: Skåne in 4 Days: Lund, Helsingborg, Kullaberg, and Österlen

visits.text: The scent of flax fills Klässbols Linneväveri, a linen weaving mill established in the village in 1920. Here you can follow the entire production process, from preparing the yarn to inspecting the finished pieces. The looms range from 19th-century handlooms to modern machines. Since 1991, the mill has supplied the linens for the Nobel banquet in Stockholm: around 500 m of tablecloth and 1,350 napkins. From May through September, the workshop and store are open daily.

days_plan.itin_title: Värmland and Dalsland in 4 Days: Canal, Aqueduct, and Forests

visits.text: The waters of Lake Vänern lap against the gates of Köpmannebro Lock, the first lock on the Dalsland Canal. It takes boats from Lake Vänern into Lake Svanefjorden. It is also the largest lock on the canal: 35.6 m long and 7.1 m wide, the same dimensions as the locks on the Göta Canal, Sweden’s other major canal. Passing through takes only about ten minutes because the difference in water levels is very small. When the lock is operating, its café sells ice cream.

activities.text: Walk from Köpmannebro to the island of Lindön: a tunnel passes beneath the railroad tracks, then a path follows the embankment. Near Lindön Lighthouse, a rocky knoll offers a view of Lake Vänern. Plants typical of limestone soils grow on the slabs of schist along the shore. The neighboring island of Långön is also accessible on foot. Mellerud station, served by SJ trains to Gothenburg and Karlstad, is about ten minutes away by car.

days_plan.itin_title: Värmland and Dalsland in 4 Days: Canal, Aqueduct, and Forests

visits.text: The heat hits you as soon as you enter the glassblowing hall at Kosta Glasbruk. Furnaces have been burning in Kosta since 1742, making it Sweden’s oldest glassworks still in operation. Its name combines the first syllables of its two founders’ names, Koskull and Staël von Holstein. About 25 glassblowers work here across five workshops. You can visit the hall daily from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. for 70 kronor per adult: avoid 11 to 11:45 a.m., when the artisans take their break.

In 1955, Kosta expanded its showroom with a glass-walled wing designed by architect Bruno Mathsson. Look down: the floor is a glass mosaic made at the glassworks. Now the Kosta Art Gallery, the space displays art pieces by Kosta Boda’s designers. Exhibitions change two or three times a year. It is open Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Sunday until 4 p.m.

Nineveh, Jerusalem, Babylon: the workers’ houses on Stora vägen, Kosta’s main street, bore the names of biblical cities. Built from the mid-18th century onward, these glassworkers’ homes were renovated in 1810 and have changed little since. Kosta’s manor house dates to 1758. Also look for Glashuset, a row of five homes designed by Bruno Mathsson, with insulating double glazing that he had patented. You can walk around the glassworks freely, at no charge.

activities.text: If you want to take home something you have blown yourself, book an introductory glassblowing session at Kosta Glasbruk. An artisan guides you step by step, and sessions start at around 500 kronor for a glass ball. In the evening, ask about hyttsill, an old glassworks tradition. You dine on herring and Småland dishes cooked in the furnaces where glass cools slowly, while watching glassblowers at work.

Drive at walking speed in your own car among the moose at Kosta Safaripark. The park covers 200 hectares of forest, roughly the size of 280 soccer fields. Bison, red deer, and wild boar also roam freely here. Book your visit through the Kingdom of Crystal booking website: prices start at 135 kronor, with free cancellation up to 24 hours in advance.

days_plan.itin_title: Småland in 4 Days: Crystal, Astrid Lindgren, and Lake Vättern

visits.text: Naturum Kosterhavet, the national park’s visitor center, stands beside the Ekenäs dock on Sydkoster. Established in 2009, Kosterhavet is Sweden’s first marine national park. More than 6,000 marine species have been recorded here, including around 200 found nowhere else in Swedish waters. Many live in the 247-meter-deep Kosterfjord trench, where the water stays cold and salty. Admission is free: dip your hands into the touch tank to feel some of the park’s inhabitants.

A staircase, a cairn, and the entire archipelago spread out before you: Valfjäll is Sydkoster’s highest hill. Its cairn, a pile of stones built at the summit, is a familiar landmark for sailors. Benches and an orientation table help you identify Nordkoster and the neighboring islands. Leave your bike near Kosters kyrka, the small church east of the hill, before climbing up.

Opened in 1939, Kosters kyrka is Sweden’s westernmost place of worship. This small church is tucked into a valley in northern Sydkoster, between the Långegärde dock and the village square. It was designed in a restrained classical style by Knut Nordenskjöld, architect to the royal court. It is open to visitors only in summer; during the rest of the year, you can only view the exterior.

activities.text: If the water beckons, walk ten minutes from the Ekenäs dock to Rörvik, where a snorkeling trail begins. Snorkeling means swimming with a mask and snorkel. The route is about 200 meters long, in water 1 to 1.5 meters deep. A blue line along the bottom leads to eight signs introducing the local animals and plants. Never swim alone, or ask someone to watch you from shore.

Rent a bike at the Ekenäs dock and ride across Sydkoster, where private cars are prohibited. Gravel paths connect the island’s three docks: Ekenäs, Långegärde, about 3.5 km away, and Kilesand, about 7 km away. You can return your bike at a different dock from the one where you rented it. Cycling is prohibited on hiking trails. For a barbecue, use only designated sites, bring your own wood or charcoal, and never use a disposable grill.

Being too high can be a problem for a lighthouse. On Högen, the highest point in the Koster Islands, the old lighthouse stood so high that fog often hid its light from sailors. In 1891, it was replaced by Ursholmen’s two towers on an islet farther offshore. To climb Högen, cross the Kostersundet strait on the small yellow cable-operated passenger ferry, then follow Nordkoster’s marked trails. The yellow trail loops around the north of the island for 5.3 km, a walk of about two hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Bohuslän in 4 Days: Marstrand, Smögen, Tanum, and Koster

visits.text: Standing 78.5 m above the sea, Kullens fyr, the lighthouse in Kullaberg Nature Reserve, is described by the reserve as the brightest in Scandinavia. Its optical system, delivered in 1900, has three large Fresnel lenses, stepped lenses that concentrate light. They rotate four times per minute, and each rotation produces three flashes, visible from about 50 km away. Right next door, the naturum Kullaberg visitor center has a saltwater aquarium. The naturum visitor center was open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. in July and August 2025.

Mölle looks like a peaceful fishing port, yet this village caused a stir in the late 19th century. Men and women swam together here, a practice considered daring at the time. This mixed bathing drew visitors from across Sweden and Europe. Until World War I, a weekly train even came from Berlin. Today, the harbor holds around 130 boats. Come at sunset, facing the Kattegat, the stretch of sea between Sweden and Denmark.

activities.text: You will follow Vandringsstigen på Västra Kullaberg, the discovery trail through the western part of Kullaberg Nature Reserve. This roughly 5 km loop starts at the naturum visitor center near the lighthouse. It passes Lahibia Cave, Ransvik Cove, the cliffs of Josefinelust, and Visit Cave at the foot of the north face. The reserve has around twenty caves. The main trail is fairly easy, but some detours down to the sea are steep: hiking shoes are essential, and take care near the cliff edges.

days_plan.itin_title: Skåne in 4 Days: Lund, Helsingborg, Kullaberg, and Österlen

visits.text: In 1621, King Gustavus Adolphus founded Gothenburg on marshy ground. Kungsportsplatsen, “King’s Gate Square,” takes its name from the main entrance through the old city walls. To build on this soft ground, the city called in Dutch engineers experienced in draining marshes. Gothenburg’s layout, with its canals, therefore follows the model of towns in Holland. The wide canal passing beneath the bridge at the square is Vallgraven, the former moat around the city walls.

activities.text: At Kungsportsplatsen, you’ll board a Paddan, an open-top boat that has been taking visitors through the canals since the 1930s. The tour lasts 50 minutes and passes under around twenty bridges, some of them very low. The boat follows Vallgraven, passing the opera house and the Feskekôrka fish market. It then heads into the harbor, passing below Läppstiftet, “the lipstick,” a tower nicknamed for its red and white stripes. The guide provides commentary in Swedish and English. All seating is outdoors: bring a jacket, even in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Gothenburg in 2 Days: Haga, Canals, Liseberg, and Styrsö

visits.text: Kungsträdgården means “the king’s garden,” but in 1430, records gave it the more modest name “the king’s vegetable garden.” In May 1971, the park witnessed the “Battle of the Elms.” Plans called for cutting down old elm trees to build a subway entrance, and residents chained themselves to the trees. The elms were saved, and the subway entrances were placed on either side of the park. In spring, 63 Japanese cherry trees planted in 1998 bloom and draw crowds. In winter, an ice rink is set up.

activities.text: Finish underground in Stockholm’s subway, often nicknamed “the world’s longest art gallery”: more than 90 of its 100 stations are decorated. Kungsträdgården station, 34 meters below ground, echoes the colors of the park’s former Baroque garden: red gravel, white marble, and green planting beds. Then take the Blue Line. At T-Centralen, blue vines surround silhouettes of the workers who built the station. Continue to Solna Centrum, where a painted forest stretches along the walls. A regular SL ticket is all you need.

days_plan.itin_title: Stockholm in 2 Days: Gamla Stan, the Vasa Museum, and Skansen

activities.text: Even if you are not a thrill seeker, Liseberg is worth an evening visit. This amusement park opened in 1923 for the exhibition celebrating Gothenburg's 300th anniversary. Thrill seekers can ride Balder, a wooden roller coaster voted the world's best in its category in 2003 and 2005 in a major international poll. Others come for the atmosphere: at Christmas, more than five million light bulbs illuminate the walkways and market. You can sip glögg, Swedish mulled wine. If you do not go on any rides, a basic admission ticket is all you need.

days_plan.itin_title: Gothenburg in 2 Days: Haga, Canals, Liseberg, and Styrsö

visits.text: The Flatruet road stops you in your tracks as soon as you leave the forest: you are at an altitude of 975 m, on Sweden's highest road, opened in 1938. Ahead lies a bare, windswept, treeless plateau - and reindeer on the road, indifferent to your car. Stop at the parking area on the crest: in clear weather, you can see Helagsfjället and its glacier to the north. The road is partly gravel and closes at night from December to mid-April.

Ljungdalen is a tiny village at the foot of Helagsfjället. It's the starting point for reaching STF Helags Fjällstation, a 12 km hike from the Kläppen car park (6 km by car from Ljungdalen). The mountain station is the base for the glacier ascent.

Helagsfjället (1,797 m) is Sweden's highest peak south of the Arctic Circle - and its slopes hold the Helags glacier, the southernmost in Sweden. The summit can be seen from afar: it dominates the surrounding landscape in spectacular fashion.

activities.text: The ascent of Helagsfjället from the mountain station is an 8 km round trip. From the summit at 1,797 m, the view extends to Sylarna in the north, Norway to the west and the Härjedalsfjällen in every direction. On the way up, you follow the southern edge of the glacier - a geological curiosity in the heart of Scandinavia. Allow 4 to 5 hours from the mountain station. Bring warm clothes even in summer: the weather changes very quickly here.

If you don't want to climb to the summit, the hike from Kläppen to the mountain station (12 km one way, Kesudalen valley and birch forest) is already very beautiful. You can stay overnight at the mountain station and return the next day. Book ahead: there are few places.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: Gammelstad kyrkstad is the world's best-preserved church town, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1996. At the centre, the stone church of Nederluleå dates from the 15th century. All around, 424 small red wooden houses (Falun red paint) were built by farmers from surrounding parishes to sleep in at weekends – distances and climate made it impossible to return home after mass. In the 17th century, isostatic rebound made the harbour too shallow for ships – the trading town moved to the coast and took the name Luleå, leaving the religious complex intact.

The visitor centre's guided tour lasts about an hour and opens doors normally closed to the public. When you're not on a tour, wander freely through the lanes between the red houses: the place is still inhabited during religious festivals like Christmas and Easter.

activities.text: The Luleå archipelago has over 1,300 islands – in summer, boats serve the main ones. Gammelstadsviken nature reserve, right next to the church town, is one of northern Sweden's best spots for observing migratory birds.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

visits.text: The finest introduction is Lunds domkyrka, Lund Cathedral. It is Romanesque in style, with rounded arches and thick walls. Its high altar was consecrated in 1145, when Lund was already the seat of an archbishop. The city was Danish at the time, as Skåne did not become Swedish until 1658. Look up at the apse, the rounded section behind the altar: its mosaic dates from 1927. The church opens daily, starting at 8 a.m. on weekdays and 9:30 a.m. on weekends.

“Finn, Finn, lay the last stone!” This cry is at the heart of the legend of Lund Cathedral’s crypt. According to the tale, the giant Finn was building the church in exchange for the monk Lars’s eyes, unless Lars could guess his name. Once his identity was revealed, Finn tried to topple the pillars in anger, but daylight turned him to stone. His statue still clings to a column. The crypt dates from 1123, and each of its 27 pillars is different. Come before noon, ahead of the crowds arriving to see the astronomical clock.

Lundagård, the large park stretching out below the cathedral, is the historic heart of Lund University, founded in 1666. At the edge of the park stands Universitetshuset, the main building, inaugurated in 1882 by King Oscar II. Look at its roof: four sphinxes stand guard there. The originals, carved from poor-quality stone, were removed in less than thirty years and replaced in the 1990s. Walk across the park: the historical museum is in the same garden.

Four enormous carved stones stand at the entrance to Historiska museet, Lund University’s historical museum. They form the Hunnestad Monument, erected around the year 1000 on Skåne’s southern coast. They include runestones, covered in inscriptions in the old Scandinavian alphabet, and stones carved with images. Lund’s tourist office describes this museum as Sweden’s second-largest archaeology museum. Check the hours: it is open only Wednesday through Sunday, from noon to 4 p.m.

Brick, stone, and half-timbering: at Kulturen, Lund’s open-air museum, moving from house to house takes you from one era to another. Opened in 1892, it brings together more than 30 historic buildings across two downtown blocks. The oldest, Dekanhuset (the dean’s house), dates from the Middle Ages. Admission costs 150 kronor per adult and is free for visitors ages 18 and under. From May to August, the museum opens daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., until 8 p.m. on Thursdays; the rest of the year, it is closed on Mondays.

Drafts are on display here, and that is the appeal of Skissernas museum, Lund’s museum of sketches. Since 1934, it has collected more than 30,000 designs for public artworks intended for squares and buildings: sculpture models and drawings for murals or reliefs. You can see how Henri Matisse, Diego Rivera, and Henry Moore prepared their commissions. The museum is closed on Mondays. Admission costs 100 kronor, but is free for visitors ages 25 and under and on Thursdays from 5 to 7 p.m.

activities.text: End the day in the peaceful surroundings of Botaniska trädgården, Lund University’s botanical garden. Established in 1690, it has occupied its current site since 1862. You can wander freely among tall trees and flower beds across its 8 hectares, roughly the size of ten soccer fields. Admission is free, and the garden opens daily from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m., so you can visit after the museums close.

If you are in the cathedral at noon, stay for the Horologium mirabile Lundense, “the marvelous clock of Lund,” built around 1425. At the top, two knights cross swords whenever the hour strikes. Then the Three Wise Men and their servants parade before the Virgin Mary. A small hidden organ plays the medieval hymn In dulci jubilo. The calendar on the dial ends in 2123, when a new one will need to be installed. The clock comes to life at noon and 3 p.m., and on Sundays at 1 p.m. and 3 p.m.

Have lunch at Saluhallen, the covered market on Mårtenstorget square in central Lund. Since 1909, this market has served as a gathering place for locals. It is a convenient stop for a quick meal between visits. On the same square, Lunds konsthall, an art exhibition hall opened in 1957, is worth a look if you have ten minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Skåne in 4 Days: Lund, Helsingborg, Kullaberg, and Österlen

visits.text: A highlight of the route is Målerås, a glassworks saved by its workers. Founded in 1890, it was bought in 1981 by designer Mats Jonasson and his colleagues to keep it running. Its specialty is animal reliefs engraved in crystal. The showroom and store are open Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and Sunday from noon to 4 p.m.

activities.text: Have lunch at Målerås Glasbruk: during the high season, the restaurant has large windows overlooking the glassblowing hall. You can eat while watching molten glass take shape. The neighboring craft center sells ceramics, jewelry, wooden objects, and local products. Then allow 1 hour 36 minutes to drive to Vimmerby.

days_plan.itin_title: Småland in 4 Days: Crystal, Astrid Lindgren, and Lake Vättern

visits.text: Start with Västra Hamnen, the former industrial port transformed into a model residential district in the 2000s. This is where the Turning Torso stands: 190 metres of twisting white concrete, designed by Santiago Calatrava and inaugurated in 2005.

Stortorget, Malmö's main central square, is framed by the 16th-century city hall and the governor's residence. Head down to Lilla Torg, the small cobbled square lined with half-timbered houses where locals gather in the evenings—it's one of the city's liveliest squares.

Malmöhus Castle dates from 1434—it's the oldest surviving Renaissance castle in Scandinavia. Today it houses several museums: natural history, art, and a section devoted to the city's history. Allow at least 1.5 hours.

The medieval old town, centered around Stortorget and Sankt Petri Cathedral (14th century), deserves an hour of wandering. Behind its austere facade, the church conceals a 16th-century Flemish altarpiece and a burial crypt.

activities.text: Late in the day, head to the Ribersborg baths: a long wooden pier extending into the sea with gender-separated bathing cabins dating from 1898. Even out of season, regulars plunge into the cold waters of the Øresund.
Walk through Möllevångstorget, the local market in the southern district, to see Malmö away from the tourist routes: vegetable stalls, spice aromas, neighborhood cafés.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand South: From Malmö to Stockholm via the Islands

visits.text: In 1909, Selma Lagerlöf became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. The following year, she used the prize money to buy back Mårbacka, the estate where she was born in 1858 and which her family had lost. Between 1921 and 1923, architect Isak Gustaf Clason enlarged the small red-painted house, turning it into a manor house. In accordance with her final wishes, the house has been preserved as it was when she died in 1940. The house can only be visited on a guided tour: 220 kronor, including admission.

activities.text: Shrubs, fruit trees, vegetable beds, and flower beds: Selma Lagerlöf created the garden at Mårbacka with horticulturist Ruth Brandberg, and the current gardener is working to restore that layout. In the 19th century, her father planted a small grove here where people would drink toddy, a hot drink made with liquor, water, and sugar. Set aside some time for the estate café, which serves homemade cakes. From June through September, admission to the garden alone costs 70 kronor.

days_plan.itin_title: Värmland and Dalsland in 4 Days: Canal, Aqueduct, and Forests

visits.text: Gripsholm Castle is worth visiting as much for the story of its royal prisoners as for its rooms. King Gustav Vasa commissioned its construction in 1537 on the shores of Lake Mälaren. From 1563 to 1567, King Erik XIV imprisoned his brother Johan and Johan’s wife here. After overthrowing Erik in 1571, Johan held him here in turn before sending him to Västerås. Don’t miss Duke Charles’s chamber, one of Sweden’s best-preserved 16th-century interiors. Allow two hours for your visit.

More than 5,300 works make up Sweden’s National Portrait Collection, housed in Gripsholm Castle. King Charles XIV John, born in France as Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte, founded it in the summer of 1822. It is described as the world’s oldest national portrait gallery. Each year, a portrait of a prominent Swede is added to the collection. Gustav III’s theater, installed in a tower in 1781, is among Europe’s best-preserved 18th-century theaters: save it for last.

“They traveled bravely far away to seek gold, and in the east they fed the eagle.” These words are carved on the Gripsholm runestone beside the castle’s approach. Feeding the eagle is a poetic image meaning to kill enemies. Tola had the stone erected for her son Harald, Ingvar’s brother. Harald had joined his brother’s expedition east between 1036 and 1041 and is believed to have died near the Caspian Sea. Stop here as you arrive at the castle.

Mariefred takes its name from Pax Mariae monastery, the “Peace of Mary,” run by Carthusians, monks who lived in silence. The monastery disappeared in 1526, when Gustav Vasa took possession of Gripsholm. The rådhus, or town hall, is a wooden house dating from 1784. Its Gustavian style is the Swedish form of late-18th-century Neoclassicism. The cemetery is the resting place of German writer Kurt Tucholsky, author of the 1931 novel Schloss Gripsholm (Gripsholm Castle). A self-guided walk of about 850 m connects these sites.

activities.text: Climb aboard the steam train of the Östra Södermanlands Järnväg, a museum railroad departing from Mariefred. Its rails are only 600 mm apart, much closer together than on a standard railroad: this is known as narrow gauge. The 11 km line connects Mariefred to Läggesta, a station served by regional trains, then continues to Taxinge-Näsby. Trains run most weekends from early May to late September, and often on weekdays in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake Mälaren in 3 Days: Drottningholm, Birka, and Gripsholm

visits.text: The most sweeping view of Marstrand takes some effort to reach: it is from Carlstens fästning, the fortress crowning the island’s highest point. King Charles X Gustav ordered construction to begin in 1658, the year the region became Swedish. It also served as a prison. Its most famous inmate, Lasse-Maja, was a thief who dressed as a woman to evade his pursuers. Sentenced to life in 1813, he was pardoned in 1839. The guided tour takes you through the kitchen where he worked. Admission: 120 Swedish kronor per adult in 2026, with guided tours in Swedish.

Glass-enclosed porches, carved wooden trim, and cobblestone streets: central Marstrand retains the look of a 19th-century seaside resort. In the 16th century, the island was one of Europe’s major herring fishing centers. When herring fishing declined, wealthy seaside vacationers sustained the island. King Oscar II was among these visitors. No cars travel on the island: wander the sloping lanes behind the waterfront, away from the bustle of the harbor.

Built between 1270 and 1319, Marstrands kyrka, Marstrand’s church, predates the fortress by more than three centuries. It probably served an order of Franciscan friars. The stone building was later expanded and remodeled several times, from 1690 to 1912. Its Baroque pulpit, carved in 1691, was given a simpler style in 1852. Opening hours vary: if the door is closed, walk around the medieval walls.

activities.text: If you arrive by car, leave it on Koön, the island opposite: cars are prohibited on Marstrandsön, the island with the fortress. The passenger ferry crosses the strait in about 2 minutes. During the day, it departs every 15 minutes; at night, it runs every 30 minutes on request. Buy your ticket on the Koön side, from the ticket machine or kiosk: it includes the return trip. Västtrafik single tickets for the region’s public transportation are not valid on board.

Walk around Marstrandsön on the 5 km coastal trail, which the tourist office estimates takes 1 hour without stops. A detour leads to Nålsögat, “the eye of the needle,” a passage between two rocks so narrow that you have to squeeze through sideways. At the tip of the island, Skallens fyr, Skallen Lighthouse, marks the point where the Skagerrak and Kattegat meet, the two seas along Sweden’s west coast. The trail alternates between rocky stretches and stairs, and trail markers are sometimes missing: wear sturdy shoes.

“Kaja” is what Marstrand residents call strolling back and forth along the waterfront, often with an ice cream in hand. The tourist office describes the island’s harbor as Sweden’s largest marina. In early July, it hosts the GKSS Match Cup Sweden, a match racing regatta in which two sailboats compete head-to-head at a time. Come in the late afternoon, when the boats return to the harbor and the waterfront comes alive.

days_plan.itin_title: Bohuslän in 4 Days: Marstrand, Smögen, Tanum, and Koster

activities.text: If the sky clears toward the end of the day, head up to Monteliusvägen, a 416-meter path clinging to the northern cliffs of Södermalm. Södermalm is the large island south of the old town. The path is named after archaeologist Oscar Montelius. The view stretches across the water to City Hall, Riddarholmen Church, and Lake Mälaren. Sunset is photographers’ favorite time here. From December through March, snow is not cleared from the path: wear shoes with good traction.

days_plan.itin_title: Stockholm in 2 Days: Gamla Stan, the Vasa Museum, and Skansen

visits.text: Lake Siljan spreads before you like an inland sea – 350 km² formed 377 million years ago by a meteorite impact, making it one of Europe's largest impact craters. Its shores are lined with wooden houses painted in dark red (the famous Falu rödfärg, a paint made from copper pigments extracted from the Falun mine) – the most quintessentially Swedish tableau imaginable.

The Zornmuseet holds the world's largest collection of works by Anders Zorn (1860–1920), a Mora-born painter who created portraits of three American presidents – Grover Cleveland, William Taft and Theodore Roosevelt. Don't miss Zorngården, his house preserved exactly as it was when his wife Emma died in 1942: guided tours in English run at 3pm Tuesday to Sunday. Allow 1.5 hours for both.

In Nusnäs, a few kilometres from Mora, you'll find the workshops where the famous Dalecarlian horses (Dalahäst) are hand-carved and painted – Sweden's unofficial symbol for generations. The craftspeople work before your eyes; it's much livelier than a museum.

On Mora's main square stands the Vasaloppet finish gate – the line that 15,000 cross-country skiers reach every first Sunday in March after 90 km from Sälen. A statue commemorates Gustav Vasa, whose ski escape in 1520 inspired the race. In 1521, the people of Mora had initially refused to join him, before changing their minds and catching up with him in Sälen to launch the uprising against the Danes.

activities.text: Cycle around Lake Siljan (Siljansleden, around 310 km for the full circuit - choose one section) or rent a kayak to paddle on its calm waters. In summer, several beaches are suitable for swimming: Siljansbadet in Rättvik is one of the best; plan a round trip by car during the day from Mora. Local providers offer rentals.

If you are here in late June, do not miss Midsommar: Dalarna is the beating heart of Sweden's Midsummer celebrations. In Leksand, on the lakeshore, more than 30,000 people gather around the leafy maypole every year - one of the country's largest celebrations. Plan a round trip by car during the day from Mora.

In the evening, stroll through central Mora – barely 10,000 inhabitants, yet packed with cafés, restaurants and craft shops. It's also the starting point of the Inlandsbanan, the legendary train that runs 1,300 km through Sweden all the way to Lapland.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: Fifteen meters of elevation change in five steps: Borenshult, northeast of central Motala, is home to the steepest lock staircase on the Göta Canal. Its five adjoining chambers connect the canal to Lake Boren, bridging a 15.3 m difference in water level. Construction took three years, and the last two locks were completed in 1825. During peak season, boats pass through one after another from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. In summer, a kiosk sells ice cream beside the locks.

Baltzar von Platen championed the Göta Canal project for nearly twenty years, but he never saw it open. This former naval officer, appointed governor-general of Norway in 1827, died in Christiania, now Oslo, on December 6, 1829. He rests in his family tomb beside the canal in Motala, at the spot he had chosen. Motala was also where the first ground was broken for the canal in May 1810.

Next, visit the Göta Canal exhibition, housed in a pavilion in the harbor district known as Dockan, between the Borenshult locks and Motala marina. It tells the story of the construction, its techniques, and its people, from Platen to Scottish engineer Thomas Telford. Across the canal lies the former site of Motala Verkstad, the workshop founded in 1822 to build machinery for the canal’s construction. The workshop later produced about 1,300 locomotives and 400 ships. The information panels are in Swedish only. Tickets are available at the nearby Mallboden café.

days_plan.itin_title: Göta Canal in 3 Days: Berg Locks, Vadstena, and Omberg

visits.text: Nordingrå Church took seven years to build and was completed in 1825 on the shore of Vågsfjärden Bay. If the door is open, look at the altarpiece, the carved panel behind the altar: it was made in Brussels. To the east are the ruins of the medieval church, whose oldest sections date from the early 13th century. Around it, twelve small church stables remain out of the roughly 80 that once stood here. Worshippers sheltered their horses in them during services, as many traveled from far away. Park near the church and explore on foot.

Mannaminne, in Häggvik, is an open-air museum, but it is far from a neatly arranged historic village: everything mingles here. Started in 1980 by artist Anders Åberg and his wife Barbro, it has more than 50 buildings on a wooded hill. You will find a Norwegian-style wooden church built in 2000, streetcars from several countries, a Stockholm subway car, and a Swedish Saab 35 Draken fighter jet. In 2026, the site was open daily from May 30 to August 31, with admission costing 180 kronor and free entry for visitors under 18. Allow at least 2 hours 30 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: High Coast in 3 Days: Skuleberget, Ulvön, and Högbonden

visits.text: Your gaze drops 100 m into the clear waters of Lake Vättern: that is the effect of Västra väggarna, Omberg’s “western walls.” At an elevation of 172 m, this viewpoint overlooks the cliffs of the wooded hill beside the lake. On Omberg, 1,700 ha of forest form an ecopark: a large area where protecting nature takes priority over timber profits. In places, the lakeside trail runs very close to the cliff edge. Hold children by the hand, especially when the ground is wet.

Alvastra kloster, at the southern foot of Omberg, is an abbey founded in 1143 by monks from Clairvaux, France. These monks belonged to the Cistercian order, the same order as the convent at Vreta. King Sverker I had given them the land. Four kings were buried here, including Sverker I himself. The abbey fell into ruin after the Protestant Reformation. The St. Klintslingan also starts at Alvastra: a 5 km loop with two steep climbs.

activities.text: Lace up your shoes at the Stocklycke parking lot, the ecopark’s visitor hub, to follow Ellen Keys led, a 6.1 km trail. It is named after the writer Ellen Key, who had her house, Strand, built at the foot of Omberg in 1910. The trail passes through beech forests: on Omberg, beech reaches its northern limit in eastern Scandinavia. A steep climb leads to Hjässan, the highest point, at just over 260 m. From there, the view stretches across Lake Vättern, Lake Tåkern, and the plain. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Göta Canal in 3 Days: Berg Locks, Vadstena, and Omberg

places.name: Örnsköldsvik

visits.text: The High Coast (Höga Kusten), listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000, is the site of the world's greatest post-glacial rebound: 20,000 years ago, 3 km of ice weighed down this land, pushing it down by 800 metres. Since the ice melted, the land has been rising by 8 mm a year - new islands regularly emerge. The High Coast suspension bridge (1,867 m), on the E4, is your gateway. From Örnsköldsvik, allow for approximately 83 km, a 1-hour drive to the bridge.

Skuleskogen National Park, established in 1984, is where this geological phenomenon is most visible. Slåttdalsskrevan is its centrepiece: a cleft 200 metres long and 40 metres deep in the red granite. The interior feels like a cathedral - the walls rise on either side and light filters down from above. Plan a return drive from Örnsköldsvik to the south entrance (Docksta), then allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the walk to the gorge and back. If you climb to the summit of Slåttdalsberget (280 m), the view over the archipelago is one of Sweden's most beautiful.

activities.text: Before or after your hike, stop at Naturum Höga Kusten at the foot of Skuleberget: the exhibition clearly explains isostatic rebound. From Örnsköldsvik, allow for approximately 36 km, a 25-minute drive. Bring sturdy footwear - the terrain is rocky and some sections are slippery.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

visits.text: Orrefors has lost its large glassworks, but not its glassblowers. Founded in 1898, the factory stopped production on July 12, 2013, when its owner moved manufacturing abroad. The Orranäs Glasbruk workshop later fired up furnaces on the site again. Its hall burned down in 2023, and a new octagonal hall was completed the following year. You can watch glassblowing up close Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

The Orrefors museum displays the glassworks’ historical collection, from early pieces to recent creations. Before glass, Orrefors depended on iron: ironworks were established here in 1726, and the glassworks later occupied their site. In Hammarsmedjan, the restored forge, you can still hear the heavy hammer that once shaped iron into bars striking. Allow half an hour for the two, then drive to Målerås, 13 minutes away.

days_plan.itin_title: Småland in 4 Days: Crystal, Astrid Lindgren, and Lake Vättern

visits.text: Östersund is the only real city on the entire circuit – 60,000 inhabitants, capital of Jämtland, founded in 1786 by King Gustav III on the shores of Storsjön. It's a jolt of modernity after the fells: cafés, restaurants, street life. Take an hour to stroll along the lake before visiting.

Jamtli is Jämtland's regional museum, 1 km north of the centre. It combines an indoor museum with an exceptional collection – including the Överhogdal tapestries, discovered 50 km north of Sveg, parts of which date back to the 9th century and constitute Europe's best-preserved Viking tapestries – and an open-air museum with historic buildings from the 18th and 19th centuries where actors in period costume have recreated peasant life every summer since 1986. The Storsjöodjuret exhibition includes the giant trap built in 1894 to capture the beast, baited with a live pig.

The island of Frösön, linked to Östersund by a bridge, is Jämtland's historic heart, long predating the city. It holds Sweden's northernmost runestone, erected between 1050 and 1080 – and the monster carved on the stone is supposed to represent the Storsjöodjuret. Legend says a wizard named Ketil Runske imprisoned the beast in the stone with a spell. Frösön church (late 12th century) has a separate bell tower typical of Jämtland – the view over Östersund and the lake from the island is the region's finest.

Along the shores of Storsjön, Storsjöodjuret statues punctuate a pleasant walk. The creature was first mentioned in writing in 1635. In 1986, for Östersund's bicentenary, it was even placed under legal protection – a law repealed in 2005. There are now 200 documented testimonies from people claiming to have seen it.

activities.text: In summer, Storsjön lends itself to kayaking and stand-up paddling – outfitters offer rentals and outings from Badhusparken. In calm weather, paddling on the lake while watching Östersund's silhouette reflected in the water has something quite surreal about it.

Östersund has been a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy since 2010 – remarkable for a city this size. In the evening, try the restaurants in the centre showcasing Jämtland products: game, mountain cheeses, wild herbs. It's the circuit's only real “city” evening.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: If you could see only one runestone in Sweden, choose Rökstenen, the Rök Stone, beside the village church. Runes are the alphabet of the ancient Scandinavians. Standing 2.4 m tall, the stone was probably carved in the early 9th century. Its roughly 760 characters form the longest known runic inscription from before Christianity. A father, Varin, honors his deceased son, Vämod, with partly coded riddles. It was found in the 19th century, embedded in the church wall. A roof has protected it since 2020. Allow 30 minutes here.

days_plan.itin_title: Göta Canal in 3 Days: Berg Locks, Vadstena, and Omberg

visits.text: You can leave your car in Barsta, a former fishing village just east of Rotsidan Nature Reserve. On the hill near the old harbor stands Barsta Chapel, built around 1650 and almost unchanged since 1699. The parish describes it as the best-preserved fishermen’s chapel in its diocese. From there, the Världsarvsleden, a 100 km hiking trail that crosses the reserve, leads to the rock slabs.

activities.text: Beneath your feet, the rock is smooth and almost flat, like an enormous slab laid beside the sea. Rotsidan Nature Reserve protects about 4 km of coastline made up of slabs of diabase, a dark rock polished by the waves. Dwarf pines and spruces grow along the edges. In the cracks grows strandtrav, a small plant found nowhere else in Sweden but this coast. During storms from the southeast, the slabs send waves surging high up the shore: stay well back from the edge.

days_plan.itin_title: High Coast in 3 Days: Skuleberget, Ulvön, and Högbonden

visits.text: The loveliest detour in the Fryken Valley is Rottneros Park, a 22 ha lakeside park filled with flowers and sculptures. Selma Lagerlöf made the estate famous as Ekeby in Gösta Berling’s Saga, her first novel, published in 1891. The old manor house burned down in 1929. Starting in 1932, miller Svante Påhlson created the park, which now holds around a hundred sculptures, including works by Swedish sculptor Carl Milles. The new manor house is private.

activities.text: If you are traveling with children, leave time for the playground at Rottneros Park, named after Nils Holgersson. He is the hero of Selma Lagerlöf’s children’s book, published in 1906 and 1907: a boy who travels across Sweden on the back of a goose. The playground follows the park’s opening hours. In the height of summer, a snack stand sells light bites, with payment by card only.

days_plan.itin_title: Värmland and Dalsland in 4 Days: Canal, Aqueduct, and Forests

visits.text: At Berga By, a small, unassuming sign marks the official starting line of the Vasaloppet – the 90 km that have connected Sälen to Mora since 1922. The inaugural race on 22 March 1922 brought together 119 skiers starting from here; the course record now stands at 3 hours 28 minutes. Setting foot on this starting line gives a tangible sense of the distance the cross-country skiers are about to cover.

The Högfjällshotellet, built in 1937, is the oldest mountain hotel in the region – and one of Sweden's most popular. Even if you're not staying here, the architecture and the view from its terrace over the snow-covered slopes (or green slopes in summer) merit a stop.

activities.text: In summer, Vasaloppsleden becomes a hiking trail along the 90 km historic route between Sälen and Mora, with eight shelters along the way. You do not have to walk it all: choose a 10 to 20 km section from Sälen towards Smågan, the race's first refreshment station.

Sälen is also Sweden's largest alpine ski area, with several resorts clustered around the massif. In summer, the pistes become mountain bike trails and local operators offer bike hire and guided descents. The region is far less crowded than in winter – make the most of it.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: In 1891, educator Artur Hazelius opened Skansen on a hill on the island of Djurgården. According to Skansen, it is the world’s oldest open-air museum: a village of historic houses brought here from across Sweden. Hazelius bought about 150 of them throughout the country to reassemble here. In the farms and houses open to visitors, hosts explain what life was like in each period. The bakery recreates an 1870s shop and sells cinnamon buns. Tickets are cheaper online. Only card payments are accepted on site.

activities.text: Next, head to the zoo area, as Skansen also showcases Scandinavia’s wild animals. Brown bears, moose, reindeer, lynx, otters, and gray seals live here. The grounds cover 30 hectares, the equivalent of about 40 soccer fields, so good walking shoes are essential. Short talks lasting 15 minutes introduce the horses and seals at times listed in Skansen’s calendar. If you’re visiting with children, add Lill-Skansen, the small children’s zoo, which is included in your ticket.

days_plan.itin_title: Stockholm in 2 Days: Gamla Stan, the Vasa Museum, and Skansen

visits.text: Despite being armed with 23 cannons, Skansen Kronan was never attacked. This small fort, whose name means “the Crown Fort,” was built between 1687 and 1700 on the hill overlooking Haga. It was intended to protect the city from a Danish attack. It later served as a prison, emergency housing, and then a military museum. Today, the interior is rented out for parties and conferences and is not open for casual visits. Head up for the view over Haga’s rooftops and downtown, especially beautiful late in the day.

days_plan.itin_title: Gothenburg in 2 Days: Haga, Canals, Liseberg, and Styrsö

visits.text: Sara Kulturhus in Skellefteå is one of the world's tallest wooden buildings: 20 storeys, 75 metres, inaugurated in September 2021. Designed by White Arkitekter, the building is constructed almost entirely from regional timber (forests within 200 km, sawmill 60 km away). It houses a theatre, museum, art gallery, library and a 205-room hotel. The glass facade reveals the raw timber structure inside – go to the top floor for views over the forests and Baltic Sea.

Bonnstan is Skellefteå's medieval church town: 116 small red wooden cabins grouped around the parish church. As at Gammelstad (which you'll see further north), these houses were used by farmers from distant parishes who stayed overnight at weekends to attend mass. Bonnstan is smaller than Gammelstad but far less touristy – you'll likely be alone in the lanes.

activities.text: The banks of the Skellefte river, which flows through town, offer a pleasant evening walk. Nordanå cultural centre, on a former estate with wooden buildings by the water, hosts temporary exhibitions and a café overlooking the river. This is where the people of Skellefteå gather in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

visits.text: About 10,500 years ago, the summit of Skuleberget was just a 9 m rock sticking out of the sea. Naturum Höga Kusten, the visitor center at the foot of the mountain, explains why. During the Ice Age, a layer of ice about 3 km thick pressed down on the region. When it melted, the land, freed of that weight, began to rise. It is still rising by about 8 mm a year. According to UNESCO, no other known place has risen as much: this is why the High Coast was listed in 2000. Admission is free.

activities.text: Climb to the summit of Skuleberget via Grottstigen, the “cave trail”: a very steep 600 m climb requiring 30 to 40 minutes of effort. A detour leads to Kungsgrottan, the King’s Cave, carved out by ice, water, and waves. It owes its name to a visit by King Charles XI in the 17th century. At the top, the 900 m Kalottstigen loop follows the ancient shoreline. It now lies 286 m above sea level: the highest ancient shoreline in the world. Head back down via the less steep Södra Bergsstigen in about 1 hour.

Swedes say vajerledsklättring, “climbing along a cable”: it is their word for via ferrata. On Skuleberget’s roughly 250 m-high east face, four climbing routes are equipped with a steel cable that you remain attached to throughout. The easiest, the white route, is the first via ferrata in Sweden and the Nordic countries: brothers Arne and Gunnar Nordin began equipping it in June 1987. Helmets and harnesses are provided on-site, with no reservation required.

days_plan.itin_title: High Coast in 3 Days: Skuleberget, Ulvön, and Högbonden

activities.text: You will then head back down into Slottsskogen, “the castle forest,” a wooded park covering 137 hectares, or nearly 190 soccer fields. Its name recalls how, when Gothenburg was founded, these woods belonged to an old fortress, Älvsborg. The zoo, free and open year-round, features Swedish animals: moose, ponies, and Gotland sheep. A pool is also home to seals and penguins. Allow 1 hour to walk around it.

days_plan.itin_title: Gothenburg in 2 Days: Haga, Canals, Liseberg, and Styrsö

visits.text: Smögenbryggan, the wooden boardwalk along Smögen’s harbor, stretches for nearly 800 meters, according to the tourist office. It is lined with sjöbodar, the sheds where fishermen once stored their gear, now converted into stores, cafés, and restaurants. Fishermen have sheltered in this harbor since the mid-16th century. In summer, it is Sweden’s busiest boardwalk: come early in the morning to see the boats without the crowds.

If you are up around 8 a.m. on a weekday, stop by the Smögens fiskauktion auction hall, Smögen’s fish auction. This is where boats unload their catch, and the public can still watch. The auction was founded in 1919 to help fishermen get a fair price. Today, it is Sweden’s second-largest fish auction. Sales take place online, with buyers from across Europe. Go on the morning of your departure, before heading to Fjällbacka.

First lit on November 1, 1842, Hållö Lighthouse is the oldest in Bohuslän, the coastal province explored on this trip. From Midsommar, the midsummer celebration in late June, through mid-August, the lighthouse and keeper’s house open daily, with guides on site. The house features exhibits on the island’s geology, flora, and fauna. Outside this period, book a guided tour by emailing the lighthouse.

Period furniture, household objects, and family photos: Fiskarstugan, the preserved fisherman’s cottage just above Smögenbryggan, shows how a Smögen family lived in the 19th century. It is maintained by the local history association, Smögens Hembygdsförening. Signs point the way from the boardwalk. The house opens only on certain summer days; during the rest of the year, visits must be requested through the association.

activities.text: Board the Hållöfärjan at Smögenbryggan: in 10 minutes, the boat takes you to Hållö, a granite island designated as a nature reserve. Its rock slabs were polished by ice during the last ice age. Near Slättehälla, a glacial pothole reaches four meters deep. This round hole was carved into the rock at the end of the ice age by meltwater flowing beneath the ice, carrying sand and gravel. In summer, the boat departs every 30 minutes, from morning until late afternoon.

The day’s most beautiful swimming spot is Marmorbassängen, “the marble pool,” a hollow among smooth rocks on the island of Hållö. A ladder leads down into clear water with turquoise hues. The tourist office ranks Hållö’s waters among the saltiest in Sweden. The saltier the water, the more buoyant you are: you will float more easily here than in fresh water. The sea stays cool even in summer, so ease into the water gradually.

“Räkmacka” is the Swedish name for an open-faced shrimp sandwich: a slice of bread covered with peeled shrimp. According to the tourist office, it may have originated in Smögen in the early 1930s, at a restaurant by the harbor. Smögen even calls itself “the seafood capital.” Try one on an outdoor patio overlooking the fishing boats. In the off-season, check opening dates: some restaurants do not reopen until April.

days_plan.itin_title: Bohuslän in 4 Days: Marstrand, Smögen, Tanum, and Koster

visits.text: Climb the 318 steps of the wooden staircase that starts at Söderköping lock and leads to the top of Ramunderberget, “Ramunder’s Mountain.” This cliff rises about 70 m above the town. From the top, the view takes in the rooftops of the old town and the Göta Canal. According to a local legend, a giant named Ramunder held a young girl named Ragnhild captive here. Benches halfway up offer a place to catch your breath. From April to September, a viewing telescope is installed in the pavilion at the summit.

Cobblestones underfoot and colorful wooden houses on either side: the Drothem neighborhood reveals Söderköping’s historic character. The town’s streets still follow their medieval layout. At its center, S:t Laurentii kyrka, St. Lawrence’s Church, was built of brick in the Gothic style in the late 13th century. Its bell tower stands separately: a 50 m wooden tower built in 1583. In summer 2026, a guided tour of the neighborhood departed from Rådhustorget square at 5:30 p.m. on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Sundays.

The Göta Canal was inaugurated at Mem, 5 km east of Söderköping, on September 26, 1832. King Charles XIV John, the former French marshal Bernadotte, attended the ceremony. Mem lock was the last lock built on the entire canal. It bridges a 3 m difference in water level between the canal and Slätbaken, a long inlet leading to the Baltic Sea. Look for the inscription from the Book of Psalms on its north wall.

activities.text: Söderköping’s best free show takes place at the lock in the canal harbor, Kanalhamnen. During peak season, from mid-June to mid-August, recreational boats pass through all day, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. A lock passage takes about 7 to 10 minutes: enough time to watch the water level change and the boat rise or fall with it. Afterward, take a seat at Smultronstället, an ice cream parlor that opened in 1982 and bills itself as Sweden’s largest ice cream restaurant. Expect to wait in line for a table; getting ice cream to go is faster.

days_plan.itin_title: Göta Canal in 3 Days: Berg Locks, Vadstena, and Omberg

visits.text: In late spring, thousands of rhododendrons bloom at Sofiero above the Øresund, the strait separating Sweden from Denmark. According to the Skåne tourist office, the park has more than 10,000 rhododendrons representing nearly 500 varieties. King Gustaf VI Adolf, a keen gardener, started this collection after receiving the estate as a wedding gift in 1905. From mid-May through late August, admission costs 155 kronor (145 online), is free for visitors age 17 and under, and can be paid by card only.

Sofiero Castle, built in the Dutch Renaissance style, was constructed in 1865 for Prince Oscar, the future King Oscar II, and his wife Sophie. Gustaf VI Adolf used it as his summer residence until 1973, then bequeathed it to the city of Helsingborg. Each season, the castle hosts an exhibition. Admission is included with the park ticket. The estate is open from late March through fall, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. through late August, then until 5 p.m. on weekdays.

days_plan.itin_title: Skåne in 4 Days: Lund, Helsingborg, Kullaberg, and Österlen

visits.text: Established in 1986, Stenshuvud National Park covers just 374 hectares, including the sea, or less than 4 km². Yet it encompasses deciduous forests, meadows, sandy heathland, and marshes. The naturum visitor center, dedicated to the park’s natural environment, is at the main entrance, signposted from Route 9. The park is home to the hazel dormouse, a small nocturnal rodent, and the European tree frog, a tiny frog that climbs trees. Stop at the naturum visitor center before your walk to get your bearings on the trails.

activities.text: If you take just one hike, choose Stenshuvud’s red trail: 2 km round-trip, about 1 hour. It passes through woods of hornbeams and old oaks, then climbs the hill. The hill has three summits; the northern one is the highest, at 97 m above sea level. From there, the view stretches across Hanö Bay. Remains of an Iron Age rampart survive near the summit. Wear sturdy shoes: the climb alternates between steps and rocky stretches.

Stenshuvud’s blue trail is a short 1 km loop, taking about 30 minutes, between the naturum visitor center and the sea. Along the waterfront, you pass Krivareboden, a former eel fishermen’s hut. This is the park’s easiest trail, adapted for people with limited mobility. Save it for the end of the day, when the climb up the hill has tired you out.

After the climb, nothing beats an hour on Stenshuvud’s sandy beach at the foot of the hill. Swimmers flock here in summer. The yellow trail, a 4 km loop taking about 1 hour 30 minutes, also leads to the beach. It passes through the arboretum at the north entrance, planted in the late 19th century, then returns through the oak forest and along the beach. Avoid sandals: this trail is very rocky in places.

days_plan.itin_title: Skåne in 4 Days: Lund, Helsingborg, Kullaberg, and Österlen

visits.text: Welcome to Gamla Stan, the birthplace of Stockholm: the old town spreads across three islands - Stadsholmen, Riddarholmen and Helgeandsholmen - between Lake Mälaren and the Baltic Sea, exactly as it was in the 13th century when Birger Jarl founded the city here in 1252. The ochre and red facades dominating Stortorget, Stockholm's oldest square, once belonged to a medieval fortress. This same square was also the site of the 1520 Stockholm Bloodbath, one of Scandinavia's most infamous political massacres. Arrive early in the morning before the tour groups - the silence of the cobbled streets at dawn is worth as much as the monuments themselves.

At the heart of Gamla Stan, the Royal Palace (Kungliga Slottet) contains over 600 rooms and remains one of the official residences of the Swedish monarch. Built in the 17th and 18th centuries in baroque style, it houses several museums including the Royal Treasury and the Tre Kronor Museum. If you're here in summer, don't miss the changing of the guard - it takes place daily at 12:15pm and is accompanied in July-August by the military mounted band.

Get lost in Mårten Trotzigs Gränd, Stockholm's narrowest alley at just 90 centimeters at its tightest point, then stroll along Österlånggatan to wander past the Hanseatic houses that recall how German merchants controlled much of Baltic trade from these walls in the Middle Ages. In the evening, Stortorget becomes one of Stockholm's best spots to dine on a terrace facing the colorful facades.

Dedicate your morning to the Vasa Museum on the island of Djurgården. The Vasa was the most imposing warship of its era: 64 cannons, 700 sculptures, 1,200 tonnes. It sank on August 10, 1628, twenty minutes after leaving Stockholm harbor, after sailing just 1,300 meters. Salvaged 98% intact in 1961 after 333 years on the harbor floor, it's now the only 17th-century vessel preserved in the world. Allow at least 2 hours and arrive at opening (8:30am in summer) to see the ship without the tour group crowds.

After the Vasa, stay on Djurgården for Skansen, an open-air museum: 160 historic buildings dismantled across Sweden and rebuilt here, creating a miniature version of 19th-century Sweden. It is also a zoo with moose, lynx and reindeer. If the weather is on your side, the island deserves a long walk along the waterfront.

In late afternoon, head to Södermalm, Stockholm's bohemian district south of Gamla Stan. Climb to Monteliusvägen for one of the finest panoramic views of the old town at sunset - locals often gather here in the evening to enjoy the view. The neighborhood is filled with vintage shops, galleries and restaurants.

Tromsø→Stockholm flight (around 2 hours 30 minutes). Back in the Swedish capital, use these final hours to discover Östermalm, a more elegant side of Stockholm than the districts visited at the beginning of your trip. Walk along Strandvägen, the grand waterfront boulevard lined with late 19th-century buildings, then head to Östermalms Saluhall, the historic covered market where stalls selling fish, cured meats, cheeses and Swedish specialties also make it a good place for lunch.

City Hall (Stadshuset, 1923) on Kungsholmen island has hosted the Nobel Prize banquet every December 10 since 1930—in the Blue Hall, which isn't blue: architect Ragnar Östberg changed his mind at the last minute and kept the red bricks exposed, but the name was already printed on the plans. The guided tour tells this anecdote.

If you still have time before your departure, return to Djurgården for one last morning surrounded by greenery, just minutes from central Stockholm. Rather than revisiting places you have already seen, discover another side of this former royal hunting ground, now covered with parks, gardens and waterfront paths.

Still on Djurgården, ABBA The Museum tells the story of the Swedish group that became a worldwide phenomenon after winning Eurovision in 1974 with Waterloo. Stage costumes, gold records, personal objects and recreated studios feature throughout a highly interactive visit: you can, among other things, sing alongside avatars of the band and virtually try on some of their costumes.

East of Djurgården, the Museum of Ethnography (Etnografiska museet) houses collections devoted to the cultures of Africa, Asia, the Americas and Oceania. Ritual objects, textiles, sculptures and photographs also tell the story of explorers and Swedish ethnographic collections. A quieter and less crowded visit than the major museums in the city center.

If you are traveling with family or want to end your trip on a lighter note, Gröna Lund is Stockholm's historic amusement park, located on Djurgården's waterfront since 1883. Roller coasters, rides and attractions occupy a surprisingly compact space facing the old town. In summer, the park also hosts numerous open-air concerts.

For one last walk before leaving Stockholm, follow the Djurgårdsbrunn Canal through the most peaceful part of the island. The path follows the water between tall trees, small footbridges and old villas, away from the bustle of the museums. You can simply walk along the canal, then return toward the center according to the time you have before heading to Arlanda.

activities.text: Settle in and spend the evening dining in Gamla Stan or Södermalm—this is your first night in Scandinavia, so take your time. Tomorrow you'll have a full day in Stockholm before boarding the overnight train.

To understand why Stockholm is built on 14 islands, take a ferry from Nybroviken to Vaxholm (45 min) or the archipelago islands. In summer, some Stockholmers swim directly from the rocks. It's the best way to grasp that the city and water are one.

Tonight, board the SJ Nattåg 94 overnight train from Stockholm Central. Departure around 6pm, arrival at Abisko Östra the next day around 11am—17 hours of travel crossing all of Sweden from south to north. Book in advance: places go fast in aurora season and summer. You can choose between a seat in an open-plan car, a 6-berth couchette compartment, or a private cabin for 2–3 people. This train is a journey in itself—the landscapes between Kiruna and Abisko in the last hour are among the most beautiful of the journey.

Last evening in Stockholm: head to Fjällgatan, on the heights of Södermalm, to admire the lights of the old town, Djurgården and the islands surrounding the city center at twilight. This walk offers one last panorama of Stockholm before your departure day.
Departure from Stockholm. Arlanda airport is 40 minutes from the center by Arlanda Express from Stockholm Central. Plan to arrive 2 hours to 2 hours 30 minutes before takeoff.

visits.text: On May 7, 1697, a fire almost completely destroyed the fortified castle of Tre Kronor, the “Three Crowns.” In its place, architect Nicodemus Tessin designed the current Baroque palace, Stockholms slott. It has more than 600 rooms. It is still the king’s official residence and workplace. The ticket includes admission to the Royal Apartments and the Tre Kronor Museum, devoted to the lost castle. It also includes the Treasury, where the royal regalia—crowns, scepters, and other symbols of kingship—are displayed. Expect to pay 220 Swedish kronor, or 240 from May through September.

activities.text: If you arrive at the palace around noon, stay in the outer courtyard of Stockholms slott for the changing of the guard. Soldiers of the Royal Guards replace the previous contingent after a parade that brings them to the palace. The ceremony lasts about 40 minutes. It starts at 12:15 p.m. Monday through Saturday and at 1:15 p.m. on Sundays and public holidays. Times may change: check them the day before on the website of the Swedish Armed Forces, which provide the guard.
