visits.text: It is best to book ahead for Stockholm City Hall, the Stadshuset: entry is only possible on a guided tour at a set time. The tour lasts 45 minutes and is offered in English or Swedish. It takes you through the Blue Hall, where the Nobel Prize banquet is held. Its brick walls are not blue, however: the architect abandoned the planned blue tiles during construction. Next comes the Golden Hall, covered in more than 18 million small mosaic tiles. Tickets go on sale online one week in advance, and the ticket office opens at 8:30 a.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Stockholm in 2 Days: Gamla Stan, the Vasa Museum, and Skansen

visits.text: Coffee, spices, cheese: at Stora Saluhallen, Gothenburg’s large covered market, your nose is your first guide. The building dates from 1888–1889. Look up: iron arches support the glass roof. Around forty shops, bars, and small food counters line the aisles. Come on Saturday as early as 10 a.m. for coffee and a pastry before your boat trip, as the market is closed on Sundays.

days_plan.itin_title: Gothenburg in 2 Days: Haga, Canals, Liseberg, and Styrsö

visits.text: Storkyrkan means “the great church”: it is Stockholm’s oldest church. Near the choir, the statue of Saint George Slaying the Dragon was unveiled in 1489. Sten Sture the Elder, who ruled Sweden at the time, commissioned it after his 1471 victory over the king of Denmark. Also look for Vädersolstavlan, the “Sun Dog Painting,” the oldest color image of Stockholm. It depicts a halo seen on April 20, 1535: ice crystals in the clouds caused false suns to shine around the real one. Admission is 120 kronor, including an audio guide.

days_plan.itin_title: Stockholm in 2 Days: Gamla Stan, the Vasa Museum, and Skansen

visits.text: Two altarpieces carved in Brussels are reason enough to stop at Strängnäs Cathedral. An altarpiece is a large decorated panel placed behind the altar. Bishop Kort Rogge gave them to the church in the late 15th century. Begun around 1250 and consecrated in 1291, the cathedral is a large brick Gothic building. It also houses the tomb of King Charles IX. In summer, it opens daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with a short guided tour lasting 30 minutes at 2 p.m.

Gustav Vasa was elected king of Sweden in Strängnäs in 1523. The date of his election, June 6, is now Sweden’s National Day. Roggeborgen is the castle built during Bishop Kort Rogge’s time, between 1479 and 1501. It housed Strängnäs’s secondary school from 1626 until the 1930s, then, starting in 1968, a library affiliated with the Royal Library. View it from the outside as you follow the roughly 1 km walk suggested by the tourist office.

The cobblestones of Lillgatan, Strängnäs’s oldest street, run alongside a strip of flat stones laid for pedestrians. Around it, the red houses of the old quarter survived the great fire of 1871. On the nearby hill, the Dutch-style windmill dates from 1855: it is the sixth built on this spot. Close by, Grassagården, a 17th-century burgher’s home arranged around a courtyard, houses a museum and a café. In summer, guided tours take you inside the windmill and Grassagården.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake Mälaren in 3 Days: Drottningholm, Birka, and Gripsholm

visits.text: Strömstads kyrka, the stone church in the town center, was built in 1768 and 1769. Following a fire, it was restored between 1817 and 1822, when its bell tower was added. Inside, model ships hang from the ceiling near gilded chandeliers and brass lamps. Look up as you enter. The church is open to visitors, and concerts are held here in summer.

activities.text: Drop off your bags in Strömstad, then follow Strandpromenaden, the waterfront promenade that runs alongside Laholmsparken park and Oscarsplatsen square. The town is one of Sweden’s oldest spa resorts. As early as 1782, visitors came to drink water from the Lejonkällan spring, which was believed to treat rheumatism. For a simple dinner, the tourist office suggests buying a bag of fresh shrimp and eating them on a dock in the marina.

According to the tourist office, Korpeberget offers the best view over Strömstad’s rooftops. The name of this rocky hill means “raven mountain.” From the top, the town appears nestled between its sheltered bay and wooded hills. Head up late in the evening: in June and July, the sun sets late at this latitude, and the light lingers.

Boats to the Koster Islands leave year-round from Norra hamnen, the northern harbor, in the heart of Strömstad. The crossing takes about 45 minutes, depending on your chosen stop. Get off at Ekenäs on Sydkoster, home to the national park’s visitor center. During peak summer 2026, from June 26 to August 2, the first departure was at 6:25 a.m., with boats running throughout the day. Pay on board by card, with no cash accepted, or through the Västtrafik To Go app.

days_plan.itin_title: Bohuslän in 4 Days: Marstrand, Smögen, Tanum, and Koster

visits.text: Tången, Styrsö's old fishing village, has white wooden houses clustered along narrow lanes. It also has a ferry dock: if you arrived at Bratten, to the east, you can leave from here after walking across the island. Along the way, the church dating from 1752 stands in Byn (“the village”), the island's oldest hamlet. West of Tången, the bays of Sandvik and Uttervik form a sheltered inlet where the water warms quickly in the sun. Save it for a summer swim.

activities.text: You will take the tram to the port of Saltholmen, then a ferry to Styrsö, a car-free island in the southern archipelago. Its roughly 1,400 residents get around on foot, by bike, by golf cart, or on mopeds fitted with cargo platforms. From the Bratten dock, climb to Stora Rös, the island's highest point. At the summit is a Bronze Age cairn, a pile of stones raised over a grave. The view stretches across the archipelago and the harbor entrance. A single Västtrafik Zone A ticket covers both the tram and the ferry.

days_plan.itin_title: Gothenburg in 2 Days: Haga, Canals, Liseberg, and Styrsö

visits.text: Sundsvall is nicknamed Stenstaden – 'the Stone City'. On 25 June 1888, a spark from a steamboat on the Selångersån river triggered the largest urban fire in Swedish history: the entire city burned in nine hours, leaving 9,000 people homeless. The decision was made to rebuild everything in stone rather than wood. Result: 51 brick and stone buildings in neo-Renaissance style now line wide streets around Stora Torget. In 2017, Sundsvall was voted Sweden's most beautiful city.

The Kulturmagasinet, housed in four converted former harbour warehouses, contains the municipal library, Sundsvall Museum (city history and the fire) and a photography museum. It's the cultural heart of the city – free entry for most exhibitions.

Climb Norra Berget, the northern hill (141 m), for the panorama over the city, sea inlets and bridges. An open-air museum at the summit presents the region's history and culture. The trail from the centre is steep but short – 20 minutes' climb.

activities.text: In the evening, stroll through Stenstaden at sunset – the brick facades take on a golden hue. The fountain in Vängåvan park, created in 1886 (two years before the fire and miraculously intact), depicts lions, dolphins and bears – animals most Sundsvall residents of the time had never seen.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

visits.text: Sundsbergs gård, an 18th-century estate near downtown Sunne, served as the model for the Björne estate in Gösta Berling’s Saga. The novel begins with a ball at Ekeby, now Rottneros, and ends here. Sunne itself appears in Selma Lagerlöf’s books as Broby. In 1893, a fire devastated the main house, and the family moved into the wing. That wing now houses the museum. The café and gallery open Wednesday through Sunday, until 4 p.m.

activities.text: Head up Tossebergsklätten, a hill north of Sunne, toward the end of the day. The narrow, steep road climbs more than 200 m in just over 2 km. At the summit, 342 m above sea level, an observation tower overlooks the Fryken Valley. You will see its long, narrow lakes. Sunne is built on the strait connecting two of them, Övre Fryken and Mellan-Fryken. The summit café opens for the season in May.

days_plan.itin_title: Värmland and Dalsland in 4 Days: Canal, Aqueduct, and Forests

visits.text: You'll arrive in Sveg through seemingly endless forests – Härjedalen is Sweden's least populated province, and you feel it. At the main crossroads, you'll come straight upon it: the giant wooden bear standing 13 m tall, weighing 80 tonnes, built between 2003 and 2005 using 570,000 nails. It has become the symbol of the town and the entire province. The brown bear is Härjedalen's emblematic animal – and the province has one of Sweden's highest densities of brown bears.
Gammelgården in Sveg is an open-air museum run by the Härjedalen handicrafts association, founded in 1913. It brings together historic buildings from the region and presents local culture.

Sveg's Inlandsbanan station is a stop on the legendary line that connects Kristinehamn to Gällivare over 1,300 km through central Sweden. The Inlandsbanan only runs in summer (June-August), one train daily in each direction. If you're passing in July, go watch the train depart.

activities.text: Sonfjället National Park, 80 km north of Sveg, is worth an excursion. Plan a round trip by car during the day from Sveg. Its volcano-shaped silhouette can be seen from afar. It is one of Sweden's areas with the highest densities of brown bears - guides offer bear safaris at sunrise and sunset. Tracks are common even if you do not see the animal. Lilltoppen (around 1,000 m) can be reached without major difficulties from the northern entrance.

Alternatively, Björnberget, the local mountain 8 km from central Sveg, offers a pleasant half-day walk with views over Härjedalen's forests and hills. In the evening, Sveg is the sleepy provincial capital – 2,500 inhabitants – but the atmosphere is authentic, with no tourist artifice.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: Ulvö gamla kapell, the old chapel on Ulvön, dates to 1622. At the time, fishermen from Gävle, a coastal town farther south, spent every summer on the island fishing for herring. In 1719, painter Roland Johansson Öberg covered the interior with scenes from the Bible in a simple folk style. In 1888, demolition of the chapel had been authorized. Two years later, King Oscar II donated 200 riksdaler, the currency of the time, during a visit to help save it. In summer, free guided visits are available from noon to 3 p.m.

Small, but the best first stop on the island: the Ulvön museum recreates a 20th-century fisherman’s home. You can see his boathouse and gistvall, the meadow where nets were spread out to dry. Screens tell the story of fishing and the salting houses, workshops where fish were salted. Ulvön is where the tradition of surströmming began in the 16th century: fermented Baltic herring with a very strong smell. Admission is free.

activities.text: Climb Lotsberget, the hill overlooking Ulvöhamn, the harbor village. The trail climbs almost continuously, largely via a staircase. At the top, the view stretches across Ulvöhamn’s wooden houses and the islands of the archipelago. The village lines the Ulvösund strait, which separates Norra Ulvön, the northern island, from Södra Ulvön, the southern island. Go up in the late afternoon, after the excursion boats have left: you will have the view almost to yourself.

If you have half a day to spare, rent a bike and head to Sandviken at the northern tip of Ulvön. This fishing hamlet, protected since 2005, is considered the best preserved in Ångermanland, the province along this coast. Around twenty gray cabins, rebuilt after a fire in 1786, line a bay with white sand. The sjöbodar, waterfront cabins, were used to store fish and nets. Families lived in the kokhus, the house where the cooking was done. A chapel dating to 1867, with a separate bell tower, overlooks the bay.

days_plan.itin_title: High Coast in 3 Days: Skuleberget, Ulvön, and Högbonden

visits.text: Umeå is nicknamed 'the City of Birches' – after a devastating fire in 1888 (the same day as Sundsvall's, 25 June), thousands of birches were planted as firebreaks. They still line the main avenues and give the city a unique appearance in autumn when the leaves turn yellow. With 90,000 inhabitants and a large university, it's northern Sweden's biggest city and served as European Capital of Culture in 2014.

Västerbottens Museum traces the region's history with emphasis on Sami culture and the forest industry. Outside, an open-air museum with old farms and buildings. Guitars – The Museum, opened in 2014, displays over 500 vintage guitars including pieces that belonged to famous musicians. Allow an hour per museum.

activities.text: Umeå has a surprisingly lively café scene for its latitude - students keep the city buzzing. Fika (a Swedish coffee break with a pastry) is almost a sport here. Walk along the Umeälven in the evening: the waterfront is lively in summer. If you have an extra half-day, the island of Norrbyskär reveals a former 19th-century sawmill village in an archipelago setting: allow for a drive from Umeå to the departure quay, followed by a boat crossing.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

visits.text: Humid heat and bird calls: Universeum's tropical rainforest transports you to another world within a few steps. This science center, which opened next to Liseberg in 2001, houses sloths, monkeys, and tropical birds in a large hall. Farther on, a 1.4-million-liter tank, more than half the capacity of an Olympic swimming pool, is home to sharks and tropical fish. A touch pool lets you touch rays. The other floors explore the human body, chemistry, and space through hands-on experiments. Buy your ticket online: it costs 30 SEK less than at the ticket counter.

days_plan.itin_title: Gothenburg in 2 Days: Haga, Canals, Liseberg, and Styrsö

visits.text: On the way to Uppsala, stop in Sigtuna, Sweden's oldest town (founded around 980). From Uppsala, allow for approximately 31 km, a 35-minute drive. Its lanes beside Lake Mälaren, ruined medieval churches and runestones make it a worthwhile stop for a good hour. St Mary's Church, built in Gothic brick, is the best preserved.

Uppsala Cathedral, completed in 1435, is the largest church in Scandinavia – 118-metre neo-Gothic spires. Inside lie the tombs of Gustav Vasa and Carl Linnaeus. Facing the cathedral, the Gustavianum houses a 17th-century anatomical theatre and Anders Celsius's original thermometer.

Linnaeus Garden (Linnéträdgården) is the botanical garden Carl Linnaeus directed from 1743 to 1778 – here he developed his method for classifying living organisms. Linnaeus's adjoining house preserves his insect collections and notes. Allow an hour for both.

Gamla Uppsala, 5 km north, is the cradle of the Swedish nation. Three great royal burial mounds from the 6th century rise on a plain – climb the tallest for the view. A small 12th-century church was built on the foundations of an ancient pagan temple described in medieval chronicles.

activities.text: End the day by the Fyrisån river in central Uppsala – cafés with waterside terraces. If you're there on 30 April (Valborg), tens of thousands of students descend a hill throwing their white caps – a centuries-old tradition.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

visits.text: In our view, the castle, Vadstena slott, deserves the most time in Vadstena. This Renaissance castle, surrounded by moats (ditches filled with water), stands on the shores of Lake Vättern. King Gustav Vasa had it built as a fortress starting in 1545. His son, Duke Magnus, later transformed it into a palace. In 1552, Gustav Vasa held his wedding banquet here after marrying Katarina Stenbock. In 2026, the castle was open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. from July 6 to August 16. In summer, the wedding hall is used for opera and is closed to visitors.

Klosterkyrkan, the church of Vadstena Abbey, was built according to the instructions of Birgitta, or Bridget of Sweden, who founded her religious order here in 1346. Consecrated on February 16, 1430, it has a nave and two aisles of equal height beneath fifteen vaults. It is nicknamed the Blue Church, and its massive limestone structure does indeed have bluish hues. In the chancel, a reliquary contains remains of Birgitta and her daughter Katarina. Admission costs 30 kronor. In summer, the church is open from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. on weekdays.

In the 1260s, King Valdemar had a palace built in Vadstena for political meetings and court festivities. This building, one of the oldest surviving in Sweden, houses the Sancta Birgitta Klostermuseum, the abbey museum. In 1346, King Magnus Eriksson and Queen Blanka donated it to establish the convent, which closed in 1595 during the Protestant Reformation. The museum recounts these centuries and the legacy of St. Bridget. From June to August, it is open daily; adult admission costs 110 kronor.

As you cross Rådhustorget, the town hall square and Vadstena’s oldest square, stop in front of the Rådhuset. It is Sweden’s oldest town hall. It was built in the early 15th century, shortly after Vadstena received its town charter in 1400. This charter gave the settlement the right to trade and govern itself. Between the abbey and the castle, stroll among the preserved historic houses. The town museum offers free admission and is open in the afternoons in summer.

Swedes call bobbin lace knyppling. It is made by crossing threads wound around small bobbins. Vadstena has remained a center for the finest lace. The Vadstena Lace Museum, which opened in 2005, tells its story. Around 1870, about 800 people in Vadstena and neighboring parishes earned their living from this work. When machine-made lace threatened this craft, lace-making schools were founded in 1903. In summer, the museum is open from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m., with admission costing 20 kronor.

activities.text: End the day beside Lake Vättern, Sweden’s second-largest lake after Lake Vänern. Its water is known for its clarity: many lakeside municipalities draw their drinking water from it. Walk along the waterfront near the castle. Vadstena lies on the lake’s eastern shore, so the sun sets over the water right in front of you.

days_plan.itin_title: Göta Canal in 3 Days: Berg Locks, Vadstena, and Omberg

visits.text: Entering the Vasamuseet is a jaw-dropping experience: a 69-meter warship towers beneath the roof. The Vasa sank on August 10, 1628, after sailing 1,300 meters: too much weight high up made it unstable. It was raised in 1961 after 333 years on the bottom. The shipworm, a mollusk that devours wood, does not live in the Baltic’s low-salinity water. This partly explains why more than 98% of the ship is original. A 25-minute guided tour is included in the ticket.

days_plan.itin_title: Stockholm in 2 Days: Gamla Stan, the Vasa Museum, and Skansen

visits.text: Although driven from the throne by his brother, King Erik XIV rests in a black marble sarcophagus in Västerås Cathedral. Gustav III provided this more dignified burial place in 1797. According to tradition, the cathedral was consecrated in 1271. Its tower, topped with a Baroque spire designed in 1694 by Nicodemus Tessin the Younger, rises to about 90 m. Take time to examine its 15th- and 16th-century altarpieces, including the one in St. Mary’s Chapel, carved in Antwerp around 1515.

Kyrkbacken, or “Church Hill,” extends north of Västerås Cathedral. Its cobblestone lanes, such as Skvallergränd, or “Gossip Alley,” follow a layout inherited from the Middle Ages. The small houses mostly date from the 18th and 19th centuries. Look for Mästermans källa: according to tradition, this small spring was reserved for the town’s executioner, who was forbidden to draw water from the public well. Many houses are occupied: respect private courtyards and wear sturdy shoes for the cobblestones.

If you add just one more landmark, choose Västerås Castle, built on a rise above the city. Gustav Vasa seized and rebuilt it: it took on its current appearance in the mid-16th century. The deposed King Erik XIV was held here from 1573 to 1575, after his captivity at Gripsholm. Admire it from the outside, then follow the Svartån, the river that flows through the city before emptying into Lake Mälaren.

Head north to Vallby Open-Air Museum, or Vallby friluftsmuseum, about 2 km from central Västerås. Around forty historic houses and farms from Västmanland, the region around Västerås, have been brought together here. Heritage livestock breeds live on the grounds, including Hedemora chickens and Jämtland goats. The estate’s manor house was completed in 1702. Admission to the grounds is generally free, with fees charged only for certain activities: come in summer, when the most activities are offered.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake Mälaren in 3 Days: Drottningholm, Birka, and Gripsholm

visits.text: Before watching glassblowing, it helps to understand what you are seeing. The Swedish Glass Museum, housed in the Smålands museum in Växjö, traces the country’s glassmaking from antiquity to “studio glass,” one-of-a-kind pieces that artists blow in their own studios. The Smålands museum is described as Sweden’s oldest county museum (regional museum). Admission is 150 kronor per adult and free for visitors ages 18 and under. The museum is closed on Mondays.

activities.text: Start your road trip in Växjö, the most convenient gateway to the route. You can arrive by train or fly from Stockholm-Bromma: the airport is about ten kilometers northwest of town. Rent your car here, since Kosta is just a 42-minute drive away. The route ends in Jönköping: if you need to return the car in Växjö, Krösatåg regional trains connect the two cities.

days_plan.itin_title: Småland in 4 Days: Crystal, Astrid Lindgren, and Lake Vättern

visits.text: Astrid Lindgren was born in 1907 on Näs farm, then on the outskirts of Vimmerby. The Astrid Lindgrens Näs center was built on the very spot where she grew up, a few minutes’ walk from the main square. Its major exhibition is called “Astrid Lindgren and the Power of Stories.” Continue your visit in the gardens. In 2027, the site is open daily from May 21 to September 26.

The bed where Astrid Lindgren was born, the harmonium, a cushion she embroidered: her childhood home at Näs is still furnished as it was when she was a child. The family still owns it, and entry is by guided tour only. The tour lasts about 45 minutes, with visitors standing throughout, and is limited to 12 people ages 8 and up. English tours are also offered from May to September. Book as soon as tickets for 2027 go on sale.

Sit across from Astrid Lindgren on Stora torget, Vimmerby’s main square. Marie-Louise Ekman’s bronze statue, unveiled in 2007, shows her at her typewriter, with an empty chair opposite for visitors. Then head down Storgatan, the main street, which still follows its medieval route, and explore the cobblestone lanes around the square, including Båtsmansbacken. Astrid Lindgren is buried in the family grave in the town cemetery.

If your children could see only one setting at Astrid Lindgrens Värld, the theme park devoted to the writer’s stories, it would be Villa Villekulla. This is the home of Pippi Longstocking, whom Swedes call Pippi Långstrump. According to the park’s 2026 schedule, Pippi performed here six times a day. Bring a raincoat instead of an umbrella, as umbrellas are prohibited during performances.

Katthult was the very first house in the park, which opened in 1981 under the name Sagobyn, “the storybook village.” It is the farm where Emil lives, the mischievous boy French readers knew as Zozo la tornade. It was built at one-third of its actual size, as were all the sets built afterward, putting them on a child’s scale. Emil performed here five times a day in 2026: note the showtimes as soon as you enter, as the park covers 18 hectares.

Here, humor gives way to adventure. Mattis’s Castle provides the setting for Ronia, the Robber’s Daughter, and Cherry Valley for the story of The Brothers Lionheart. In 2026, each of these two settings hosted four shows a day. One of the park’s shows, “The Day of the Battle,” includes frightening scenes and effects. The park recommends it for ages 9 and up: check the program before settling in with young children.

activities.text: Plan your day around the shows at Astrid Lindgrens Värld: the 2026 program included 28 daily performances, from 10:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. They are performed in Swedish, so tell the children the stories before you go. In 2026, a one-day ticket in peak season cost 565 kronor per adult and 430 per child, with free admission for children under 3. The park’s stores and restaurants do not accept cash. In 2027, the park is open daily from May 21 to August 22.

The best moment of the day is not always a show. Between performances, let the children try the “Don’t Touch the Ground” trail, where they make their way along without setting foot on the ground. The Tiny Town, the play barn, and the hamlet of Bullerbyn, drawn from another series of books, round out this vast playground. There are plenty of picnic areas: securely close any bags left in your stroller, as the park’s birds help themselves.

days_plan.itin_title: Småland in 4 Days: Crystal, Astrid Lindgren, and Lake Vättern
Småland in 4 Days: Crystal, Astrid Lindgren, and Lake Vättern

visits.text: This morning, cross back over the Öland Bridge to the mainland, then drive north to Oskarshamn (~80 km from the bridge, about 1 hour). This is where the ferry departs for Gotland. Board a Destination Gotland ferry for a crossing of about 3 hours—book ahead in July–August, as spaces sell out quickly. Arrive in Visby by ferry from Oskarshamn. The first thing you'll see as you enter the harbor: the ramparts. These 3.4 km of medieval walls, built between the 12th and 14th centuries, rank among Northern Europe's best-preserved. UNESCO-listed since 1995, they feature 44 towers and have never been dismantled. Walk the complete circuit—allow 1.5 hours.

Visby's ruined medieval churches are among the town's most distinctive features. Gotland had 16 churches for a town of just a few thousand inhabitants in the Middle Ages—most were abandoned after 1361 when Danish King Valdemar Atterdag captured the city. The ruins of St. Catherine's (Franciscan, 13th century) and St. Nicholas are the most photogenic.

Fiskargränd, the “fishermen's lane,” is covered with blooming roses from June to August. It's one of Gotland's most photographed lanes—narrow, cobbled, with low houses whose gardens overflow onto the lane.

Gotland Museum (Gotlands Museum) holds the world's largest collection of painted rune stones—these slabs illustrated with mythological scenes date from the 5th to 11th centuries. The treasury section displays thousands of Viking-era coins found in the island's fields.

From Visby, head by road to the north of Gotland, then take the ferry to Fårö, the small island north of Gotland (free crossing, 5 minutes). This is where Ingmar Bergman lived and worked from 1967 until his death in 2007 - he filmed several works here, including Persona and Scenes from a Marriage. The house is visible from the outside; a centre devoted to his work organises screenings in summer. Plan this as a day trip with a return journey.

The raukar of Fårö are limestone columns sculpted by marine erosion over thousands of years. These strange formations, 3 to 6 metres high, stand on the island's beaches and heathland like petrified figures. The most accessible are at Langhammars and Digerhuvud. From Visby, allow for a day trip with a return journey by road and the ferry crossing to Fårö.

Gotland has more than 90 rural medieval churches, some dating back to the 11th century. They look similar from the outside - limestone walls, a square tower, interior paintings - but each hides different details. The churches at Gothem, Garde and Roma are among the most remarkable and can be visited freely. From Visby, allow for a round trip by road to Gothem and Garde.

activities.text: In the evening, Visby comes alive around Stortorget and the lanes of the center within the walls. Restaurants set up outdoor seating in the courtyards of medieval houses—it's an atmosphere quite different from the rest of Sweden.

If you arrive in summer (early to mid-August), check the dates of Visby's Medieval Week (Medeltidsveckan): it is one of Europe's largest medieval festivals, with costumes, jousting and markets throughout the old town.

From Visby, reach Fårö by road and then by ferry for this day trip. Rent a bicycle on Fårö to link the wild beaches and the raukar - the island is small (about 30 km long) and has few visitors. Sudersand is the most beautiful beach, with white sand and water that can reach 20°C in July.
Back in Visby in the evening, climb the northern ramparts to watch the sun descend over the Baltic Sea—in summer, light lingers until 10 PM.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand South: From Malmö to Stockholm via the Islands
The Grand South: From Malmö to Stockholm via the Islands

visits.text: Prisoners of war are often blamed for setting fire to Visingsborg, but the tourist office tells a different story. On the evening of December 22, 1718, a sergeant named Johan Rasch burned some straw from his mattress in the stove to light his pipe. The fire broke out later. Only the south wing remains of the Brahe family’s castle, completed in 1662 after nearly a century of construction. The ruins are right next to the harbor: you can walk around them freely, but you cannot go inside the walls, which are at risk of collapse.

Climb the narrow, steep staircase in the bell tower of Kumlaby kyrka, a church dating from the early 12th century. In 1636, Per Brahe the Younger had the spire shortened to install a platform at the top for observing the stars. On a clear day, you can see four Swedish provinces from there. Inside, the wall paintings date from the 15th and 17th centuries. The church is open daily from mid-June to mid-August, and admission costs 20 kronor per adult.

The ruins of Näs, at the southern tip of Visingsö, are the remains of Sweden’s first royal castle. In the 12th century, the Sverker dynasty made it their residence, and four Swedish kings died on the island. The castle was destroyed in 1318. The tourist office recommends having a picnic there overlooking the lake: pick up a packed lunch at the harbor’s fish shop before you set off.

activities.text: Cycling is still the best way to see Visingsö: the island is 14 km long, and its narrow roads are mostly paved, with a few gravel stretches. Rent a bike at the harbor, then head south toward the oak forest. The Swedish navy began planting it in 1831 to provide timber for its warships. By the time the trees were large enough, ships were being built from other materials, and the forest remained.

days_plan.itin_title: Småland in 4 Days: Crystal, Astrid Lindgren, and Lake Vättern

visits.text: Take time to study the Vitlycke rock panel, the most visited of the Tanum rock carvings, which were UNESCO-listed in 1994. Nearly 300 figures were pecked into this rock surface, about 22 meters high, by repeatedly striking the stone. They include ships, people, animals, and a bridal couple, the best-known carving in Bohuslän. The oldest date to around 1800 BCE. Never walk on the rock: it is fragile.

Vitlycke Museum, a few hundred meters from the rock panel, is the visitor center for the listed site. Inside, Bronze Age figures have been reconstructed based on excavations of graves and settlements. Outside, a reconstructed farm has two longhouses and a workshop. In summer, crafts from the period are practiced here. The museum is most active during the warmer months, and its hours vary by month: check its website before visiting. Admission is free for visitors under 20.

About 2 km from the museum, the Litsleby rock panel is nicknamed “the panel of the spear god.” A giant brandishing a spear towers over the other figures. The tourist office describes it as Scandinavia’s largest carved human figure. A wheelchair-accessible ramp lets you get close and take photographs without stepping onto the rock. A tactile panel also describes it through touch.

Musicians, dancers, warriors, hunters, deer, and dogs crowd the Fossum rock panel, about 4 km from the museum. Ships frame the densely packed scenes. They may tell a story of gods and goddesses. You can also spot a female figure known as the Fossum woman. About 100 meters to the east, the Balken carving shows a horse pulling the sun: take the detour on foot.

activities.text: If you have another hour, follow the Aspeberget trail, about 800 meters from the museum: a route just under a kilometer long links its carved rock panels. The three largest are painted red to help visitors make out the lines. This practice is criticized because it changes the rock’s original appearance. The very fragile bull panel remains covered for most of the year. Unpainted carvings are easier to make out early in the morning or late in the day, when low-angle light highlights their grooves.

days_plan.itin_title: Bohuslän in 4 Days: Marstrand, Smögen, Tanum, and Koster

visits.text: On the road between Malmö and Ystad, make a detour to Smygehuk: it is Sweden's southernmost point, marked by a small red-and-white striped lighthouse on a rocky coast. Nothing spectacular - but it is the country's geographical extremity. From Ystad, allow for a round trip by road for this visit.

Ystad is a well-preserved medieval town with cobbled lanes, tightly packed half-timbered houses, and a 13th-century Franciscan monastery, Klostret, now converted into a regional museum. Fans of the Wallander crime series will recognize the settings—exteriors were filmed here.

Do not miss Ales Stenar at Kåseberga, approximately 19 km from Ystad, a 20-minute drive to the village followed by a walk uphill to the monument. This megalithic monument of 59 standing stones forms a 67-metre ellipse shaped like a Viking ship on a grassy cliff facing the Baltic Sea. Built around AD 600, its exact purpose remains debated - a solar observatory, burial site, or commemorative monument. The sea view at sunset is one of the finest in Scania.

activities.text: Head up to the fishing village of Kåseberga at the foot of the cliff to see the boats hauled onto the shore and the traditional eel smokehouses - smoked eel is a local speciality. From Ystad, allow approximately 19 km, a 20-minute drive to the village.
In the evening in Ystad, walk along Stora Östergatan, the best-preserved street in the medieval center, and look for a café in one of the hidden courtyards behind the facades.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand South: From Malmö to Stockholm via the Islands
